papers.title: Field-level modeling of halo and galaxy alignments
papers.authors: Nickolas Kokron, Mikhail M. Ivanov, James M. Sullivan
papers.abstract: We develop an effective field theory (EFT) of intrinsic alignments at the level of spin-2 field fluctuations of large-scale structure tracers, such as the shapes of galaxies and dark matter halos. Our perturbative model includes the non-linear treatment of the Zel'dovich displacement, and contains all necessary shape operators through the third order. We apply our field-level model to the full 3D distribution of galaxy shapes, whose sky projections are a known contaminant of cosmic shear measurements. Our field-level EFT model achieves a better description of the helicity fields of dark matter halo shapes than the standard non-linear alignment (NLA) and tidal torquing + tidal alignment (TATT) models in the literature, as evidenced by improved correlations with the simulations' initial conditions. We perform precision measurements of field-level bias parameters by means of a generalized least-squares problem, for which we derive an optimal estimator and analytic covariance matrices. We measure the full set of linear, quadratic, and cubic shape bias coefficients as a function of halo mass in the $\texttt{Quijote}$ N-body simulations. We then study the intrinsic alignments of galaxies in the $\texttt{FLAMINGO}$ hydrodynamical simulation, focusing on observationally relevant samples: spirals, ellipticals, luminous red galaxies (LRG) and emission-line galaxies (ELG). We detect linear and nonlinear alignment coefficients at high significance for LRG, spiral and elliptical galaxies. We also find evidence for non-zero density-weighted tidal bias coefficient of the simulated ELG. This work supports the notion that EFT-based models of alignments will be paramount in optimally extracting constraints from future shape correlations, and lays the foundation for the development of simulation-based priors for future galaxy shape samples.

conclusions: The field-level cubic spin-2 EFT basis reduces from 11 to 10 independent operators (showing $s^2 s_{ab}$ is redundant even at the field level) and achieves a much higher cross-correlation with simulated 3D halo shape helicity fields ($m=0, \pm 1, \pm 2$) than standard NLA or TATT models, yielding median reduced $\chi^2 \approx 1$ on perturbative scales.

Recasting the field-level comparison as a generalized least-squares (GLS) problem provides an optimal, cosmic-variance-canceling estimator with an analytic covariance matrix that closely matches the ensemble covariance across 50 Quijote simulation boxes.

In Quijote, all 10 shape bias coefficients are measured as a function of halo mass, showing consistent values with 1-loop power spectrum fits; tidal torquing and velocity shear coefficients ($c_{\mathcal{G}^s}, c_t$) as well as 1-loop cubic coefficients ($c_{\mathcal{G}^{(3a)}}, c_{\mathcal{G}^{(3b)}}, c_{L_3}$) vary non-monotonically with mass and change sign around $|c_s| \gtrsim 0.1$.

In the high-resolution FLAMINGO hydrodynamical box (L1_m8), the field-level estimator recovers LRG alignment amplitudes with similar signal-to-noise as Quijote despite a $20\times$ smaller volume, detects strong linear, density-weighted, and tidal-torquing alignments in spiral and elliptical galaxies, and finds evidence for a non-zero density-weighted tidal bias in emission-line galaxies (ELGs).
ai.relevance_reason: Directly builds upon the shifted-operator Lagrangian field-level bias framework (by Nickolas Kokron and collaborators) central to your highest-relevance research profile, extending it from scalar galaxy density to spin-2 intrinsic alignment fields.
ai.summary: Because galaxy and halo shapes are stretched and torqued by surrounding matter, their orientations correlate across large scales—a phenomenon called intrinsic alignments (IA) that both contaminates weak lensing cosmic shear measurements and carries cosmological information. While standard IA models like non-linear alignment (NLA) and tidal alignment plus tidal torquing (TATT) only include the lowest-order tidal effects and are typically fitted to two-point summary statistics, a complete Effective Field Theory (EFT) description requires higher-order spin-2 (quadrupole shape) operators whose numerous nuisance parameters are hard to constrain from power spectra alone. In this paper, the authors develop a 3D field-level EFT model for spin-2 shape fluctuations up to third order in perturbation theory, constructing Lagrangian shape operators from the initial density and tidal fields and advecting them to late times using Zel'dovich displacements ("shifted operators") decomposed into a spherical harmonic helicity basis. By formulating a cosmic-variance-canceling generalized least-squares estimator on the 3D grids of the Quijote N-body and FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations, they directly measure all 10 independent linear, quadratic, and cubic shape bias parameters for halos and realistic galaxy types (LRGs, ELGs, spirals, and ellipticals), laying the groundwork for informative simulation-based priors in weak lensing surveys like Euclid.

papers.title: Two-dimensional galaxy cluster shapes using lensing data: a simulated analysis
papers.authors: C. Giocoli, M. Meneghetti, G. Despali, L. Moscardini, E. Rasia, G. Lesci, W. Cui, G. Yepes
papers.abstract: Context. Cluster morphology reflects assembly history and dynamical state. High-resolution weak lensing can reveal departures from spherical symmetry, but its ability to recover two-dimensional shapes remains less explored. Aims. We assess how reliably weak lensing recovers projected cluster morphology and its dependence on orientation and dynamical state. We also compare large-scale weak-lensing morphology with that traced by strong lensing near the cluster centre. Methods. We study three clusters at $z=0.22$ from The Three Hundred Project, representing relaxed, mildly disturbed and unrelaxed systems. For each, we consider three random projections and three along the principal axes of the mass tensor. For each projection, we generate 128 weak-lensing catalogues with a source density of 30 arcmin$^{-2}$ and intrinsic ellipticity dispersion $\sigma_{\epsilon}=0.3$. We constrain mass and concentration from one-dimensional NFW and BMO fits, then recover ellipticity, position angle and centre using a two-dimensional elliptical NFW model. We also measure morphology from true convergence maps, Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions and strong-lensing tangential critical lines. Results. Recovered parameters depend on orientation and dynamical state. The relaxed cluster has similar inner and large-scale shapes, whereas disturbed systems appear more elliptical centrally. Two-dimensional weak-lensing modelling recovers the projected mass orientation despite source sampling and shape noise. Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions recover the position angle well but favour rounder mass distributions. Centroid offsets are larger in unrelaxed systems. Conclusions. Combining weak- and strong-lensing morphology probes cluster structure across physical scales and offers a promising way to investigate morphology and dynamical state.

conclusions: Two-dimensional elliptical NFW modelling of realistic weak-lensing shear catalogues ($n_{\rm gal}=30\,{\rm arcmin}^{-2}$, $\sigma_\epsilon=0.3$) reliably recovers the projected position angle of individual clusters despite source sampling and intrinsic shape noise.

Imposing Gaussian priors on cluster mass ($M_{200}$) and concentration ($c_{200}$) derived from 1D circular NFW fits systematically lowers the inferred 2D ellipticity, demonstrating a significant covariance between assumed radial profiles and recovered halo shapes.

In the relaxed cluster ($\eta=0.998$, centre-of-mass offset $\Delta_r=0.017$), the inner strong-lensing critical lines and outer weak-lensing maps show consistent shapes and orientations, whereas disturbed clusters ($\Delta_r$ up to $0.238$) appear significantly more elliptical in their cores than on larger scales and exhibit larger centroid offsets.

Non-parametric Kaiser & Squires (KS93) convergence reconstructions accurately recover the projected orientation angle of the clusters, but systematically bias the mass distribution towards rounder shapes due to smoothing and noise dilution.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides background context on weak-lensing mass and morphology modelling for galaxy clusters in upcoming surveys like Euclid, though it focuses on standard $\Lambda$CDM hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM theory, emulators, or large-scale structure perturbation theory.
ai.summary: Because dark matter haloes assemble by accreting matter along cosmic web filaments, galaxy clusters are intrinsically triaxial (elongated like a rugby ball) rather than spherical, and their exact shapes reflect whether they are dynamically relaxed or actively merging. Standard weak-lensing analyses average the distortion of background galaxies in circular rings around a cluster to estimate its mass, which throws away information about its 2D projected shape and orientation. The authors test how well full 2D weak-lensing shear modelling can recover projected cluster morphology by selecting three clusters at $z=0.22$ from The Three Hundred hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations—representing relaxed, mildly disturbed, and strongly merging systems—and viewing each along six lines of sight (three random and three aligned with the 3D mass tensor axes). By generating 128 mock weak-lensing catalogues per projection (with a Euclid-like source density of $30\,{\rm arcmin}^{-2}$) and comparing 2D elliptical NFW fits and Kaiser & Squires mass reconstructions against inner strong-lensing critical lines, they show that joint weak- and strong-lensing analyses can trace how cluster shapes and orientations twist from the core to the outskirts in disturbed systems.

papers.title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
papers.authors: Pulkit Sheoran, Ankita Bera, Sultan Hassan
papers.abstract: The escape fraction of ionizing photons, $f_{\rm esc}$, is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, $f_{\rm esc}(z)$, $f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h})$, and $f_{\rm esc}(z, M_{\rm h})$, against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow $f_{\rm esc}$ to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant-$f_{\rm esc}$ model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from $\approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$. The halo-mass-only model prefers $f_{\rm esc}$ increasing with halo mass, but this trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent $f_{\rm esc}$. At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$. These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the $f_{\rm esc}$ prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Ly$\alpha$ and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

conclusions: To prevent the abundant early JWST galaxies from reionizing the universe too early, the data strongly require an effective escape fraction that decreases toward higher redshift, falling from $f_{\rm esc} \approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$ (with power-law redshift index $b_z \approx -0.90$).

While a halo-mass-only model prefers $f_{\rm esc}$ increasing with halo mass ($b_m = 1.83^{+0.23}_{-0.28}$), this acts merely as a proxy for redshift evolution because lower-mass halos dominate at earlier times; when redshift and halo mass are varied jointly, the mass dependence vanishes ($b_m = 0.09^{+0.32}_{-0.17}$).

At a fixed global neutral hydrogen fraction, all four $f_{\rm esc}$ prescriptions (including a constant $f_{\rm esc}$) yield virtually identical 3D ionization bubble morphologies and reach the same reionization milestones within $\Delta z \lesssim 0.4$ of one another.

The resulting 21 cm brightness temperature power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$ across all models at matched ionization stages, meaning that standard global observables and two-point 21 cm statistics cannot distinguish how $f_{\rm esc}$ is distributed across galaxies once calibrated to the same global history.
ai.summary: During the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), ultraviolet photons from the first stars and galaxies ionized the neutral intergalactic medium (IGM), but recent JWST discoveries of surprisingly abundant, UV-bright galaxies at $z \gtrsim 9$ have created a "photon budget crisis": if a standard fraction of their ionizing photons escaped into the IGM, reionization would have finished much earlier than allowed by CMB optical depth and Lyman-$\alpha$ forest measurements. The key bottleneck is the ionizing photon escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$)—the proportion of ionizing photons that survive absorption by dense gas and dust inside their host galaxies—which cannot be measured directly at high redshift because the neutral IGM is opaque. In this paper, the authors test whether varying $f_{\rm esc}$ as a power law in redshift, halo mass, or both can resolve this tension by fitting semi-analytic source models via MCMC to JWST UV luminosity functions, IGM neutral fraction data, ionizing emissivity, and the Planck Thomson optical depth ($\tau$), and then propagating the best-fit prescriptions into the semi-numerical simulation `SimFast21` (which uses the Zel'dovich approximation and excursion-set halo finding). This matters because it reveals that while declining high-$z$ escape fractions naturally reconcile JWST galaxy counts with reionization timelines, small-scale interstellar medium physics governing $f_{\rm esc}$ largely averages out on cosmological scales, leaving the 3D ionization bubble morphology and 21 cm power spectrum nearly indistinguishable across parameterizations.

papers.title: ECH0EZ: Estimating the Hubble constant with ZTF SN Ia DR2
papers.authors: Konstantin Karchev, Marco Giunta, Raul Jimenez, Roberto Trotta, Licia Verde
papers.abstract: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are instrumental for a precise measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) from the local distance ladder, yet the data used hitherto for this purpose are inhomogeneous and subject to severe selection effects. We present the first, preliminary, cosmological analysis of 772 SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release: an untargeted single-telescope sample whose volume-limited subset (z<0.06) is largely free of Malmquist bias. We correct the public data for known instrumental and calibration biases and the redshifts for peculiar motions. Using the 42 SH0ES calibrators (their host distances computed from Cepheids and geometric anchors) and a Bayesian hierarchical model of SN Ia standardisation, dust extinction, redshift and calibration uncertainties, we infer $H_0 = (71.6 \pm 1.5)$ km/s/Mpc after marginalising over deceleration with a flat prior (or $(72.3 \pm 1.1)$ km/s/Mpc if a prior on matter density from Pantheon+ is imposed), with the uncertainty dominated by the number of calibrators. We demonstrate robustness to the choice of light-curve and Milky Way dust models and to extensions of the model to include peculiar-velocity correlations, a host-mass step, and two stretch populations. These results are in agreement with previous distance-ladder measurements and $2.7\sigma$ ($4.1\sigma$) away from the value obtained from Planck data, suggesting that the resolution of the Hubble tension lies outside of SNe Ia---or the distance ladder entirely.

conclusions: Using 772 ZTF DR2 supernovae and 42 SH0ES Cepheid calibrators, the authors measure $H_0 = 71.6 \pm 1.5\text{ km/s/Mpc}$ when marginalising over the deceleration parameter $q_0$ with a flat prior, which is in $2.7\sigma$ tension with Planck $\Lambda$CDM.

Imposing a Pantheon+ prior on the matter density tightens the constraint to $H_0 = 72.3 \pm 1.1\text{ km/s/Mpc}$, increasing the tension with Planck to $4.1\sigma$ and demonstrating that replacing heterogeneous Hubble-flow SN samples with a uniform, volume-limited ZTF sample does not lower $H_0$.

The inferred $H_0$ is highly robust against systematic model variations, including different light-curve fitters, Milky Way dust maps, peculiar-velocity covariance models, a host-galaxy mass step, and bimodal SN stretch populations.

The dominant source of uncertainty remains the small sample size of Cepheid-calibrated host galaxies (42 SNe), meaning future improvements in local $H_0$ precision require more calibrators rather than larger Hubble-flow SN catalogs.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the Hubble tension (listed under medium relevance in your profile) by testing whether selection biases and sample inhomogeneity in Hubble-flow SNe Ia can explain the discrepancy between local and CMB $H_0$ measurements.
ai.summary: Measuring the local Hubble constant ($H_0$) via the cosmic distance ladder relies on Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) in the smooth Hubble flow, but traditional compilations combine data from many different telescopes with complex, brightness-dependent selection effects (Malmquist bias). To test whether these observational inhomogeneities drive the Hubble tension, the authors perform the first cosmological analysis of 772 SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility Second Data Release (ZTF DR2), an untargeted, single-instrument survey that provides a nearly complete, volume-limited sample at $z < 0.06$. They anchor this uniform Hubble-flow sample to 42 SH0ES Cepheid-calibrated SNe and use a Bayesian hierarchical model (`ECH0EZ`) to jointly infer $H_0$ alongside supernova standardization parameters, dust extinction, calibration offsets, and peculiar velocity corrections. Their resulting $H_0$ values agree closely with SH0ES and remain in significant tension with Planck, showing that Hubble-flow supernova selection effects and multi-survey calibration systematics are unlikely to explain the Hubble tension.

papers.title: All Dark Matter as Primordial Black Holes: a Gravitational-Wave Test
papers.authors: A. Ianniccari, A. J. Iovino, G. Perna, D. Perrone, A. Riotto
papers.abstract: We propose a novel test for the hypothesis that the dark matter of the Universe is composed entirely by asteroidal-mass primordial black holes. It relies on detecting the stochastic gravitational-wave background generated by the coalescence onto rapidly spinning supermassive astrophysical black holes of the light primordial black holes accumulated in spherically symmetric spikes. We discuss the scenarios in which the signal can be observed by the future space-based gravitational-wave observatories LISA and DECIGO.

conclusions: In the fiducial analysis (SMBH masses $5 \times 10^5\,M_\odot \leq M \leq 10^7\,M_\odot$, dimensionless spin $\chi = 0.95$, PBH mass $m = 10^{-11}\,M_\odot$), LISA can detect the stochastic GW background only if the dark matter spike power-law slope exceeds $\gamma = 2.5$ (the maximum slope produced by standard adiabatic SMBH growth), though including omitted polar harmonic modes and the full SMBH mass range could bring $\gamma = 2.5$ within reach.

The next-generation space interferometer DECIGO is sensitive enough to detect the PBH inspiral background across all tested parameter configurations, with its higher-frequency band strongly probing lighter SMBHs ($10^4\,M_\odot \leq M \leq 5 \times 10^5\,M_\odot$) whose spin distribution will shape the spectrum.

An analytical approximation restricted to equatorial prograde orbits ($x = \cos\iota = 1$) captures the spectral shape and high-spin boost of the full inclination-averaged numerical result, whereas using the Newtonian quadrupole flux formula near the innermost stable orbit overestimates the true relativistic Teukolsky flux peak by roughly a factor of 8.
ai.summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs)—hypothetical black holes formed from early-Universe density fluctuations rather than stellar collapse—can still make up 100% of dark matter in the 'asteroidal-mass window' ($10^{-16}\,M_\odot \lesssim m \lesssim 10^{-11}\,M_\odot$), where they are too heavy to have evaporated via Hawking radiation and too light to be ruled out by gravitational microlensing due to finite-source wave effects. If dark matter consists entirely of these asteroidal-mass PBHs, adiabatic growth of central supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in galaxies draws them into steep central density cusps ('spikes'), where they undergo extreme mass-ratio inspirals ($q = m/M \sim 10^{-22}\text{--}10^{-17}$) into the SMBH. While individual inspirals are far too faint to resolve, the authors compute the incoherent superposition of gravitational waves (GWs) emitted across all galaxies—solving the relativistic Teukolsky equation for generic inclined spherical orbits in Kerr spacetime and integrating over the cosmic SMBH mass function—to predict the resulting millihertz stochastic GW background. This provides a formation-independent observational test for asteroidal-mass PBH dark matter using future space-based GW detectors like LISA and DECIGO.

papers.title: Non-minimal $α$-attractor magnetogenesis with potential dependent couplings
papers.authors: Antonino G. Marino, Tommaso Mengoni
papers.abstract: We investigate inflationary magnetogenesis driven by a non conformal coupling in the case of large-field $\alpha$-attractor inspired models. We introduce potential-dependent electromagnetic coupling functions $f(\phi)$ that reproduce the scaling $f\propto a^p$ during slow roll. Starting from Starobinsky inflation, we analytically derive explicit couplings for $(E)$-model and $(T)$-model potentials. We then study how these functions affect electromagnetic amplification in the regime of non-minimal coupling between the inflaton field and the Ricci scalar $\phi^2 R$. In particular, we compare different values for the coupling strength $\xi$, accounting for electromagnetic backreaction and Schwinger pair production through the gradient expansion formalism. Our numerical results show that the non-minimal coupling affects the evolution of the electromagnetic sector and the resulting magnetic-field amplitude. We find that, within the analyzed configurations, minimally coupled and $\xi>0$ scenarios are compatible with the adopted CMB constraints, yielding conditional present-day magnetic-field estimates of order $10^{-23}$ G.

conclusions: Derived explicit, analytical inflaton-photon coupling functions $f(\phi)$ for $E$-model and $T$-model $\alpha$-attractor potentials that maintain $f \propto a^{-5/2}$ during slow roll and approach $f(0) = 1$ at the end of inflation to avoid strong coupling.

Negative non-minimal gravitational couplings ($\xi < 0$) yield stronger magnetic fields by delaying electromagnetic amplification, but are ruled out by Planck CMB bounds because their scalar spectral index $n_s$ is too red.

Minimally coupled ($\xi = 0$) and positively coupled ($\xi > 0$) configurations satisfy CMB constraints on $n_s$ and $r$, producing conditional present-day magnetic field seeds of order $B_0 \sim 10^{-23}\,\text{G}$ (assuming adiabatic $a^{-2}$ dilution without modeling reheating), which are too weak on their own to fully explain intergalactic magnetic fields without further astrophysical dynamo amplification.
ai.summary: Explaining the origin of large-scale cosmic magnetic fields via primordial inflation—a process called inflationary magnetogenesis—requires breaking the conformal invariance of electromagnetism so that quantum vacuum fluctuations can be amplified rather than diluted by cosmic expansion. In this paper, the authors construct kinetic coupling functions $f(\phi)$ between the inflaton field and the electromagnetic sector tailored to $\alpha$-attractor inflationary potentials (specifically Starobinsky, $E$-models, and $T$-models) so that the coupling scales as a power law with the scale factor ($f \propto a^p$) during slow roll and smoothly restores standard electromagnetism ($f \to 1$) after inflation. They also include a weak non-minimal coupling $\xi \phi^2 R$ between the inflaton and gravity, and solve the coupled background and electromagnetic evolution numerically using the Gradient Expansion Formalism (which tracks spatial averages of electromagnetic bilinears via a truncated ODE hierarchy). Crucially, their setup accounts for both electromagnetic energy backreaction on the expansion history and the Schwinger effect, where strong electric fields spontaneously create charged particle-antiparticle pairs that damp the fields. This provides a self-consistent test of whether popular $\alpha$-attractor inflation models can simultaneously satisfy Planck CMB constraints and generate viable seed fields for present-day intergalactic magnetism.

papers.title: Towards Reliably Measuring the Mass-Size Relation of Dark Matter Halos: Impact of projection, miscentering and Eddington bias
papers.authors: Charlie T. Mpetha, Benedikt Diemer
papers.abstract: In the conventional spherical overdensity definition of a dark matter halo, masses and radii, e.g. $M_{200{\rm m}}$ and $r_{200{\rm m}}$, are equivalent. However, halos do exhibit a physical boundary at the splashback radius $r_{\rm sp}$, which manifests as a sharp drop in density. Splashback radii are now routinely measured in stacked weak lensing profiles, but the expected trend of decreasing $r_{\rm sp}/r_{200{\rm m}}$ with mass has not been verified in observed galaxy groups or clusters. In this work, we show that several observational effects conceal the predicted mass-size relation. In particular, we quantify the impact of systematics on the mean density and lensing profiles of mock-observed halo samples, which are created by applying a realistic cluster-finding procedure to dark matter-only simulations. We reproduce the known impact of projection: preferentially observing systems in overdense regions. But, differing from previous works, we show that the same projection effect, combined with scatter in observed luminosities, causes a significant Eddington bias in the derived mass-observable relation and a complex suppression in mean density profiles over all radial scales. The magnitude of this effect is mass-dependent and coupled to the cluster-finding procedure and survey properties, making it challenging to model simply and motivating full forward-modeling of observed group and cluster samples. However, we demonstrate that a simple mitigation approach, effectively a weak lensing mass calibration, does well in approximately recovering the true mass-size relation. Finally, we show that only severe miscentering can bias the measurement of the halo size, but any miscentering can increase the measurement uncertainty.

conclusions: Luminosity scatter (Eddington bias) is the largest single effect, suppressing mean density profiles by up to ~30%. Photo-z projection effects cause a similar suppression.

Combined realistic systematics suppress mean profiles by up to ~40% and shift the recovered halo radii by similar amounts. This is likely why the expected mass-size trend has not been seen in observations.
Even scatter-free abundance matching changes the mean profiles by up to ~10% relative to the truth sample.
Only severe miscentering biases the measured halo size, but any miscentering increases the uncertainty.

Rescaling profiles by the known mean mass of each bin, which is effectively a weak-lensing mass calibration, approximately recovers the true mass-size relation. This was tested assuming a perfect mass tracer.
ai.summary: Dark matter halos have a physical edge, the splashback radius, where the density drops sharply. It is the apocenter of the first orbit of infalling matter. Simulations predict that $r_{\rm sp}/r_{200{\rm m}}$ falls with halo peak height $\nu$ (a redshift-independent mass measure). Stacked weak-lensing measurements of galaxy groups and clusters have not confirmed this trend. The authors built mock cluster catalogs from the dark-matter-only Erebos N-body suite at $z\approx0.4$. They assigned luminosities by abundance matching and ran simplified luminosity-based and richness-based (redMaPPer-like) cluster finders. These finders include projection effects (photo-z and spec-z) and luminosity scatter. They then computed mean density and lensing profiles, added miscentering with a neural-network emulator, and fitted a truncation-radius profile model. Scatter in observed luminosity, combined with projection, produces an Eddington bias (low-mass halos scatter into higher-mass bins) that suppresses the mean profiles. This bias is dominant and depends on both mass and the cluster finder, so full forward-modelling of cluster catalogs is needed.

papers.title: Warm inflation beyond the Gaussian limit: primordial black holes and induced gravitational waves
papers.authors: Mayukh R. Gangopadhyay, Nilanjana Kumar
papers.abstract: In warm inflation, the primordial fluctuations are driven by random kicks from a hot radiation bath. Two features of these kicks matter: how long the bath remembers them, which shapes the power spectrum, and how their strengths are spread, which controls the rare, extreme fluctuations. In this paper, we investigate how primordial black holes and the accompanying induced gravitational waves can be used to discriminate between these two features. We use a simple model inspired by warm inflation, in which independent kicks of random strength add up to a narrow peak in the power spectrum. At leading order, the induced gravitational wave depends only on the power spectrum and is therefore insensitive to how the kicks are distributed. However, the black holes are very sensitive to these rare large fluctuations. Hence, two baths can yield the same gravitational wave signal while forming black holes at very different rates. A modest kurtosis range of 0.1 to 0.3 enhances black-hole formation by factors of ten to a million at fixed gravitational-wave amplitude, the larger factors for the rarer black holes. Counting peaks rather than all points, or widening the spectrum, lowers the enhancement by at most a factor of about four. In general a change in the power affects both phenomena, while the kurtosis affects only the black hole production.

conclusions: Two thermal baths with identical power spectra produce the same leading-order scalar-induced gravitational wave (SIGW) spectrum, which scales strictly as $\Omega_{\text{GW}} \propto A^2$ regardless of the higher-order statistics of the thermal kicks.

A modest positive excess kurtosis of $\kappa \in [0.1, 0.3]$ in the curvature perturbation distribution enhances PBH abundance by factors of $10$ to $10^6$ at a fixed gravitational-wave amplitude, because heavy tails dramatically boost the probability of crossing the collapse threshold $\zeta_c$.

More realistic calculations—such as counting physical density peaks rather than simple threshold crossings (Press–Schechter) or widening the power spectrum peak—reduce this non-Gaussian enhancement by at most a factor of $\sim 4$.

Combining SIGW observations (which constrain the variance $A$) with PBH abundance bounds (which constrain both $A$ and the tail kurtosis $\kappa$) breaks the degeneracy between the thermal bath's memory time and the non-Gaussian distribution of its kick strengths.
ai.summary: In "warm inflation" scenarios, the inflaton field continuously interacts with a hot radiation bath during inflation, meaning primordial curvature perturbations are sourced by random thermal kicks rather than pure quantum vacuum fluctuations. The authors investigate how to observationally disentangle two key microscopic properties of this thermal bath: its memory time (which shapes the overall power spectrum peak) and the probability distribution of the kick strengths (which governs the non-Gaussian tails of rare, extreme fluctuations). Using a toy model where independent thermal kicks build up a narrow peak in the primordial power spectrum, they compute both the resulting scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs, generated at second order when large density modes re-enter the horizon) and the abundance of primordial black holes (PBHs, formed from the gravitational collapse of extreme overdensities). Because SIGWs depend on typical fluctuations while PBHs depend exponentially on the extreme upper tail of the probability distribution, combining both observables allows cosmologists to separate the variance of the thermal noise from its non-Gaussian kurtosis.

papers.title: Relativistic N-body simulations with mass-varying neutrinos
papers.authors: Øyvind Christiansen, Julian Adamek, Mainak Baidya, Vitor da Fonseca, Eric V. Linder, David F. Mota
papers.abstract: Recent cosmological data provide weak hints for smaller masses than what is required by neutrino-oscillation experiments, motivating investigations into variation of the neutrino masses with cosmic time. Here we study a model where the neutrinos couple to a quintessence field that acts as dark energy. We compute structure formation using fully dynamical and relativistic N-body and lattice simulations, with nonlinear field evolution and a weak-field metric expansion. Similar to previous studies, we find the generic appearance of neutrino lumps, but observe them to be highly dynamical and spinning. We study several models where the effective dark energy, including nonlinear effects of the scalar field on the cosmic expansion, can show phantom crossing. The relativistic physics available in our simulation framework can help distinguish such models from LCDM, through observations of neutrino and dark energy properties, and slip between the gravitational potentials due to anisotropic stress. The rich phenomenology offered by mass-varying neutrinos motivates further exploration and development of the simulation techniques.

conclusions: In the constant-coupling scaling quintessence model, non-linear backreaction and rapid scalar oscillations can initially delay, weaken, or dissipate catastrophic "neutrino lumps", yielding highly dynamical and spinning neutrino structures instead of static overdensities.

Coupling neutrinos to quintessence allows them to remain effectively massless for most of cosmic history (evading early-universe cosmological upper bounds like $\sum m_\nu < 0.064\,\mathrm{eV}$ from DESI+CMB) while growing to match laboratory oscillation minimums ($\sum m_\nu > 0.06\,\mathrm{eV}$) today.

Energy transfer and non-linear scalar field backreaction on the cosmic expansion rate induce an effective dark energy equation of state $w_{\mathrm{eff}}$ that oscillates across the phantom divide ($w = -1$).

While cold dark matter clustering can remain broadly consistent with $\Lambda$CDM, the coupled system generates distinctive gravitational slip ($\Phi \neq \Psi$) from neutrino anisotropic stress and significant modifications to the Weyl lensing potential, making weak lensing and ISW probes with Euclid and LSST key discriminators.
ai.relevance_reason: This paper presents relativistic N-body simulations (extending gevolution/AsGRD) of a beyond-$\Lambda$CDM dark sector including backreaction on the expansion history, directly aligning with your focus on relativistic N-body methods, beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations, and backreaction (plus co-authors from ITA Oslo).
ai.summary: Recent cosmological constraints from DESI and the CMB push the upper bound on the sum of neutrino masses ($\sum m_\nu \lesssim 0.06\,\mathrm{eV}$) uncomfortably close to—or even below—the minimum floor required by terrestrial neutrino oscillation experiments, motivating Mass-Varying Neutrino (MaVaN) models where neutrino masses grow over cosmic time via coupling to a quintessence dark energy scalar field. Historically, such models have been plagued by severe fifth-force instabilities that cause neutrinos to collapse into massive, unphysical non-linear structures ("neutrino lumps"). To study this non-perturbative regime accurately, the authors introduce `GAsGRD`, a GPU-accelerated, relativistic N-body and lattice simulation code built on `gevolution-2.0` that solves the coupled neutrino-scalar-gravity system using an ADM $3+1$ formulation capable of handling large conformal factor variations and backreaction on the background expansion. They show that in a constant-coupling scaling quintessence model, fully dynamical relativistic effects and large-scale scalar backreaction can naturally weaken or dissipate neutrino lumps, keep cold dark matter clustering close to $\Lambda$CDM, and produce phantom-crossing effective dark energy, while leaving clear signatures in the gravitational lensing potential and anisotropic stress.

papers.title: Cosmological constraints on single-field inflation models from ACT/SPT data and observations at sub-Mpc scales
papers.authors: Qing-Yang Wang, Jing-Zhi Zhou, Fei-Yu Chen, Zhi-Chao Li
papers.abstract: We investigate single-field inflation models that can produce large curvature perturbations at sub-Mpc scales while remaining consistent with cosmological observations across multiple regimes. We highlight the tension between generating enhanced small-scale perturbations and maintaining agreement with the scalar spectral index $n_s$ measured by ACT and SPT, which disfavors several conventional single-field inflation models. To address this issue, we propose three viable classes of inflationary potentials: bump/dip-modified, step-like, and double-inflection-point. Each can sufficiently amplify primordial perturbations while predicting $n_s$ that lie within the $2\sigma$ range of current observational bounds. In addition, we examine the primordial power spectra predicted by these models and constrain their parameter spaces using cosmological observations at different scales, including CMB, BAO, PBH, PTA, and CMB-distortion. Our results show that some of the models considered can simultaneously satisfy the ACT/SPT constraints and account for the current PTA observations, although doing so while respecting the constraints on the PBH abundance remains challenging.

conclusions: All three inflation classes possess parameter regions that amplify the small-scale primordial power spectrum to $\mathcal{P}_\zeta \sim 10^{-2}$ (the level needed to source observable gravitational waves) while keeping the large-scale spectral index $n_s$ within $2\sigma$ of the ACT/SPT bounds ($n_s \approx 0.973 - 0.974$).

When fitted to the NANOGrav 15-year data, the step-modified Starobinsky potential fails to match the broadband spectral shape of the gravitational-wave signal, being strongly disfavored relative to astrophysical supermassive black hole binaries ($\ln \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{SIGW}}_{\mathrm{SMBHB}} \simeq -25$).

The bump/dip-modified KKLT and double-inflection-point models fit the NANOGrav spectrum well (with $\ln \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{SIGW}}_{\mathrm{SMBHB}} \simeq +3.1$ for the latter), but $82.3\%$ to $96.3\%$ of their PTA-favored posterior parameter space is ruled out because the required perturbation amplitudes overproduce primordial black holes ($f_{\mathrm{pbh}} > 1$).

Consequently, none of the three single-field inflation scenarios can simultaneously dominate the observed nanohertz gravitational-wave background and satisfy all multi-scale cosmological bounds across their main posterior volume.
ai.summary: In single-field inflation, generating large primordial curvature perturbations on sub-Mpc scales—which can collapse into primordial black holes (PBHs) and source second-order scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs)—usually requires a brief "ultra-slow-roll" phase where the inflaton slows down on a flat feature in its potential. However, spending $e$-folds in ultra-slow-roll shortens the standard slow-roll regime, typically lowering the predicted large-scale scalar spectral index $n_s$ well below the high values ($n_s \approx 0.973 - 0.974$) recently measured by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and South Pole Telescope (SPT). To resolve this tension, the authors construct and numerically evolve three classes of modified inflationary potentials—a Gaussian bump/dip on a string-inspired KKLT potential, a multi-step Starobinsky potential, and a polynomial double-inflection-point potential—testing them against multi-scale constraints from CMB anisotropies, BAO bounds on radiation density, COBE/FIRAS CMB spectral distortions ($\mu$ and $y$), PBH overproduction, and the NANOGrav 15-year Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) nanohertz gravitational-wave signal. They show that while all three potential classes can reconcile small-scale amplification with the ACT/SPT $n_s$ bounds, explaining the observed PTA background with SIGWs remains nearly impossible without overproducing PBHs.

papers.title: Getting Ready For Analysing Rubin Data : CLMM v2, The Updated LSST-DESC Cluster Weak Lensing Mass Modeling Library For Cosmology
papers.authors: Michel Aguena, Céline Combet, Shenming Fu, Constantin Payerne, Marina Ricci, Camille Avestruz, Eduardo Barroso, de Oliveira Caio, Zhou Conghao, Hsin Fan, Calum Murray, Anna Niemiec, Nikolina Sarcevic, Tae-hyeon Shin, Rance Solomon, Radhakrishnan Srinivasan, Sunayama Tomomi, Yuanyuan Zhang, Joe Zuntz
papers.abstract: The Dark Energy Science Collaboration has prepared a multitude of pipelines to process the upcoming Vera C. Rubin Observatory data and perform different scientific analyses. Here, we present the methodology to constrain the mass information of galaxy clusters from weak lensing, which is encompassed by the v2.0 release of the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling (CLMM) code. This Python library provides the ingredients for both the modeling and data reduction of lensing observables, and the improvements in the new version were customized to handle the first WL analyses of LSST clusters, including, e.g., stacking functionalities and WL multipoles. This new version of CLMM has allowed various cluster analyses using LSST-DESC simulated data, precursor survey and Rubin commissioning and survey validation data, and is ready to be used for the first cluster cosmology analyses. CLMM is an open-source software package collaboratively written in Python, providing multiple example notebooks, including a set that can reproduce all figures in this work, and extensive documentation, publicly available at this https URL .

conclusions: Introduces the `ClusterEnsemble` module to support stacked weak-lensing radial profiles across multiple clusters, including lens-source pair weighting and data-driven covariance estimation via sample, bootstrap, or healpy-based jackknife resampling.

Expands theoretical profile modeling beyond a single spherical halo by adding the 2-halo term $\Delta\Sigma_{2\text{h}}(R)$ (from surrounding correlated large-scale structure, which dominates beyond a few Mpc) and quadrupole shear components to capture halo triaxiality.

Adds key observational systematic corrections required for real data: radial boost factors $B(R)$ (power-law and NFW parameterizations) to correct for signal dilution by unlensed cluster member galaxies, single-halo miscentering offsets $R_{\text{mis}}$, and magnification bias $\delta_\mu = \mu^{\alpha-1}$.

Integrates with the `qp` library to handle full photometric redshift probability density functions (PDFs) rather than just point estimates, and interfaces directly with `CCL` and `NumCosmo` as cosmological theory backends for LSST DR1 readiness.

ai.summary: Counting galaxy clusters as a function of mass and redshift is a powerful probe of cosmic structure growth, but it requires calibrating the true total masses of clusters using weak gravitational lensing—the subtle coherent distortion of background galaxy shapes by the cluster's gravitational potential. While ideal models treat clusters as isolated, spherical halos, real optical survey data suffer from observational systematics like miscentering (picking the wrong cluster center), contamination by unlensed cluster member galaxies that dilute the shear signal, and the gravitational influence of surrounding large-scale structure. In this paper, the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC) presents version 2.0 of `CLMM` (Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling), an open-source Python library built to compute theoretical lensing profiles and reduce observed galaxy catalogs into lensing data vectors for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The authors upgrade the code from a simple single-cluster tool to a full survey-ready pipeline by adding ensemble stacking, data-driven covariance estimation, triaxial (non-spherical) halo multipoles, and realistic systematic corrections. This release provides the core mass-calibration engine for the upcoming first LSST data release (DR1) and integrates directly into the broader DESC cosmological inference pipeline.

papers.title: A self-supervised machine learning approach to identify instrumental systematics in 21cm Cosmology
papers.authors: Ajith Sampath
papers.abstract: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.

conclusions: A linear probe on the learned 2D instrument latent vector accurately predicts the unseen spectral ripple amplitude ($\mathscr{A}$) across 15 held-out test instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ (compared to $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline), showing the network isolates the physical beam systematic without explicit labels.

The learned instrument latent contains no detectable astrophysical sky signal when tested against a total-power sky proxy on held-out pointings, confirming that the drift-scan consistency loss successfully enforces sky-invariance.

Disentanglement remains asymmetric and incomplete: while the instrument latent is free of sky contamination, the sky latent vector still retains some residual instrumental imprint, making sky-latent purification the main hurdle before the method can be used for full foreground cleaning.
ai.summary: Upcoming 21cm intensity mapping surveys aim to measure Baryon Acoustic Oscillations by mapping the integrated radio emission of neutral hydrogen across large cosmic volumes, without resolving individual galaxies. However, radio interferometers measure Fourier-space sky correlations (visibilities) weighted by the antennas' directional sensitivity pattern (the primary beam); frequency-dependent ripples in this beam—known as beam chromaticity—mix ultra-bright galactic foregrounds into the faint cosmological signal. To identify these systematics without relying on an explicit instrument model or labeled training data, the author trains a self-supervised convolutional autoencoder on simulated drift-scan visibilities (for a compact $6\times 6$ dish array across 400–800 MHz). By exploiting the physical symmetry that the instrument state remains constant as the sky rotates overhead while the same sky is observed across different nights (instrument states), the network splits the data into an instrument latent vector and a sky latent vector, offering a promising step toward model-independent systematics calibration.

papers.title: Cosmological Constraints on Interacting Dark Matter with SPT-3G D1
papers.authors: Cynthia Trendafilova, Fei Ge, Ali Rida Khalife, Christian L. Reichardt
papers.abstract: Models of the dark sector in which the dark matter participates in nontrivial interactions can create detectable signatures in cosmological observables, providing non-terrestrial means of probing the nature of dark matter. In this work, we test dark matter-baryon scattering, dark matter-dark radiation interactions, and dark matter annihilation using measurements of the CMB and BAO. We leverage the latest SPT-3G D1 CMB measurements of the primary anisotropies, alongside the D1 MUSE lensing data, to set up-to-date bounds on these models. From the combination of Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data, we constrain the velocity-independent dark matter-baryon scattering cross-section to $\sigma_\mathrm{DM-b} < 4.6\times10^{-26}~\mathrm{cm^2}$, the dark matter-dark radiation momentum transfer rate to $\Gamma_\mathrm{0,nadm}<5.2\times10^{-8}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$, and the effective dark matter annihilation parameter, quantifying the fractional thermally averaged cross-section, to $p_\mathrm{ann}<3.7\times10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^3/s/GeV}$, all at the 95% confidence level. The improved sensitivity to the first two models is in particular driven by the precision measurements of CMB lensing at small scales provided by SPT-3G D1 MUSE lensing data. For annihilating dark matter, due to the degeneracy of the effect with the optical depth to reionization, we observe a non-trivial relationship between the upper bound on $p_\mathrm{ann}$ and the large-scale polarization information. When combining CMB data with the latest measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), upper bounds on extended model parameters can appear to tighten as the model space attempts to accommodate the known discrepancy between these data. Future CMB and BAO measurements will provide better clarity on reconciling this discrepancy and enhance our ability to test dark matter interactions.

conclusions: Combining Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data yields no significant evidence for dark matter interactions, setting 95% CL upper bounds on the velocity-independent DM–baryon scattering cross-section ($\sigma_\mathrm{DM-b} < 4.6 \times 10^{-26}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ for $m_\mathrm{DM}=1\,\mathrm{GeV}$), the DM–dark radiation momentum transfer rate ($\Gamma_{0,\mathrm{nadm}} < 5.2 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$), and the effective DM annihilation parameter ($p_\mathrm{ann} < 3.7 \times 10^{-28}\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}\,GeV^{-1}}$).

Adding SPT-3G D1 MUSE lensing data tightens constraints on early-time DM–baryon scattering by $\sim 30\%$ (for $n_b=0$) to $50\%$ (for $n_b=2$) and improves bounds on DM–dark radiation momentum exchange by more than $50\%$, driven by the high sensitivity of small-scale lensing ($350 \le L \le 3000$) to small-scale structure suppression.

For DM annihilation, high-resolution ground-based CMB data add little constraining power beyond Planck because energy injection mainly alters large-scale polarization, making the $p_\mathrm{ann}$ upper limit highly sensitive to the choice of low-$\ell$ $EE$ likelihood and the reionization optical depth ($\tau_\mathrm{reio}$) prior.

Adding DESI DR2 BAO data artificially tightens the upper limits across these interacting dark sector models because DESI prefers a lower $\Omega_m$ than the CMB, forcing degeneracies (and higher $\tau_\mathrm{reio}$ in the absence of tight priors) to shift the posterior toward smaller interaction parameters to accommodate the tension between the datasets.

ai.summary: While standard $\Lambda$CDM assumes dark matter is completely cold and collisionless, dark matter could participate in non-gravitational interactions—such as scattering off ordinary baryons, interacting with a relativistic "dark radiation" fluid, or annihilating into Standard Model particles—that shift the CMB acoustic peaks, inject energy around recombination, or damp small-scale matter clustering. In this paper, the authors test these three dark sector scenarios by combining primary CMB and lensing data from Planck and ACT DR6 with the new South Pole Telescope (SPT-3G D1) primary and small-scale MUSE lensing measurements, alongside DESI DR2 BAO data. They run MCMC parameter inference using `CLASS` (incorporating `HMCode` and `CLASS_PT` / EFT of LSS to model non-linear small-scale clustering) to update constraints on the interaction strengths. This matters because high-resolution CMB lensing at small angular scales ($L \le 3000$) directly probes the small-scale suppression of structure growth caused by dark matter scattering, while combining CMB and BAO data reveals how known parameter tensions between early- and late-universe probes can artificially tighten bounds on beyond-$\Lambda$CDM physics.

papers.title: Improving cosmological distance measurements at high redshift using Lyman-Alpha forest BAO reconstruction
papers.authors: Boryana Hadzhiyska, Roger de Belsunce
papers.abstract: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) measures baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in the Lyman-$\alpha$ (Lyman-alpha) forest and provides a robust probe of the expansion history in the matter-dominated era. Yet, non-linear structure formation broadens and shifts the BAO peak. To undo these effects, we extend standard Zel'dovich reconstruction, routinely applied to galaxy surveys, to the Lyman-alpha forest. We validate our methodology on large-volume idealized Lyman-alpha forest mocks painted on top of the \textsc{AbacusSummit} $N$-body simulations, using linear control variates to suppress sample variance and thereby reduce the error bars by a factor of up to $\approx \sqrt{50}$. In fully sampled periodic boxes, reconstruction halves the radial BAO damping scale and reduces the uncertainties on the radial ($\apar$) and transverse ($\aperp$) scaling parameters by $\approx25\%$ and $\approx15\%$, respectively. It also reduces the non-linear shift from $\Delta\apar=+0.3\%$ to $+0.10\pm0.07\%$, while $\aperp$ remains unbiased. To make this approach readily applicable to observational data, we demonstrate the impact of a survey mask with a DESI-like density of $50\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. For this mask, we compare two approaches to estimate the displacement field: either directly from the Lyman-alpha forest or using an external tracer with a number density of $\bar n \simeq 10^{-3}\,h^3\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, such as Lyman-break galaxies and Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters---both key targets for DESI-II. Both approaches give comparable gains and reduce the uncertainties on $\apar$ and $\aperp$ by $\approx 27\%$ and $\approx 10\%$, respectively, with mild improvements for futuristic high-density surveys with $160\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. Correspondingly, the figure of merit improves by factors of $1.66$ for fully sampled boxes, $1.65$ for a DESI-like, and $1.76$ for a high-density survey.

conclusions: In fully sampled periodic boxes, reconstruction halves the radial BAO damping scale and reduces uncertainties on the radial ($\alpha_\parallel$) and transverse ($\alpha_\perp$) BAO scaling parameters by $\approx 25\%$ and $\approx 15\%$ (precision gains of $1.34\text{--}1.40$ and $1.17\text{--}1.22$), respectively.

Using linear control variates to shrink sample variance errors by $\approx \sqrt{50}$, the authors show that reconstruction suppresses the systematic non-linear radial shift of the BAO peak from $\Delta\alpha_\parallel = +0.3\%$ down to $+0.10 \pm 0.07\%$, while keeping $\alpha_\perp$ unbiased.

For a realistic DESI-like sightline density ($50\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$), estimating displacements either directly from the sparse forest or via external galaxy tracers with $\bar{n} \simeq 10^{-3}\,h^3\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$ yields comparable uncertainty reductions of $\approx 27\%$ on $\alpha_\parallel$ and $\approx 10\%$ on $\alpha_\perp$ (an overall BAO figure-of-merit gain of $1.65$).

Reconstruction yields similar precision improvements for both the Ly-$\alpha$ auto-correlation and the Ly-$\alpha$ $\times$ quasar cross-correlation, though real-data systematics like continuum fitting (which projects out long line-of-sight modes) remain to be tested.

ai.summary: Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in the Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly-$\alpha$) forest—the dense series of neutral hydrogen absorption lines in distant quasar spectra—probe the expansion history at high redshifts ($2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4$), but non-linear bulk flows broaden and shift the BAO peak. While standard galaxy surveys routinely undo these non-linearities using Zel'dovich BAO reconstruction (shifting tracers back along an estimated large-scale displacement field), applying this to the Ly-$\alpha$ forest is tricky because it is a continuous flux field sampled sparsely across the sky and has an independent line-of-sight velocity-gradient bias ($b_\eta$) that modifies its redshift-space distortions. In this paper, the authors adapt standard Zel'dovich reconstruction to the Ly-$\alpha$ forest by solving for the linear displacement field using Either the smoothed flux decrement itself or an overlapping sample of discrete galaxy tracers (like Lyman-break galaxies expected in DESI-II), and validate the method on idealized Ly-$\alpha$ mocks painted onto the AbacusSummit $N$-body simulations at $z=2.5$. This provides a practical path to sharpen high-redshift distance constraints and remove systematic BAO shifts without having to marginalize over the many nuisance parameters of a full one-loop EFT model.

papers.title: Axions from Betelgeuse: Probing Axion Couplings with $^{23}\rm{Na}$ and $^{55}\rm{Mn}$
papers.authors: Nicholas A. M. Revel, Baldeep Grewal, Anupam Ray, Aaron C. Vincent
papers.abstract: We investigate axion-like particle (ALP) production in the interior of Betelgeuse via nuclear de-excitation of thermally populated excited states of $^{23}$Na and $^{55}$Mn. As these ALPs propagate to Earth, they can produce photons either through their conversion in the Galactic magnetic field or through their decay. Using INTEGRAL-ISGRI and NuSTAR observations, we search for these photon signals, find no significant excess, and derive 95% CL exclusion limits on the ALP couplings. For magnetic-field conversion of ALPs, the $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ ($^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$) line observed with INTEGRAL-ISGRI constrains $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}| < 4.1\times10^{-21}$ ($6.9\times10^{-19}$) $\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ for $m_a < 10^{-10} \mathrm{eV}$. For ALP decays, the $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ ($^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$) line observed with INTEGRAL-ISGRI (NuSTAR) constrains $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}|$ down to $3.0\times10^{-22}$ ($2.9\times10^{-19}$) $\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ at $m_a \simeq 400$ ($83$) keV, weakening in both cases as $m_a^{-3/2}$ for lower ALP masses, and as $m_a^{-2}$ for $^{23}$Na below $m_a \sim 1$ keV, with sensitivity extending to $m_a \simeq 440.2$ ($124$) keV. Although our $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$-based limits are the strongest for both channels, their larger transition energy makes them more sensitive to the precise evolutionary stage of Betelgeuse, whereas the $^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$-based limits are considerably more robust against such uncertainties.

conclusions: Using archival X-ray and soft gamma-ray data from NuSTAR and INTEGRAL-ISGRI, no excess photon signal is detected from Betelgeuse, placing 95% confidence level upper bounds on the product of ALP-photon and ALP-proton couplings ($|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}|$).

For ultralight ALPs ($m_a < 10^{-10}\,\text{eV}$) converting in the Galactic magnetic field, the $^{23}\text{Na}$ ($^{55}\text{Mn}$) transition constrains $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}| < 4.1 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{GeV}^{-1}$ ($6.9 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{GeV}^{-1}$), improving upon previous $^{57}\text{Fe}$ Betelgeuse bounds by two orders of magnitude for protons, though still surpassed by SN 1987A limits.

For heavier decaying ALPs ($a \to \gamma\gamma$), $^{23}\text{Na}$ constraints reach $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}| \lesssim 3.0 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{GeV}^{-1}$ at $m_a \simeq 400\,\text{keV}$ and surpass leading astrophysical bounds in the $155\text{--}440\,\text{keV}$ mass window.

Because the $440.2\,\text{keV}$ $^{23}\text{Na}$ state requires high core temperatures to be thermally populated, its limits assume Betelgeuse is near the end of core carbon burning and weaken by orders of magnitude if the star is in an earlier evolutionary stage, whereas the $125.9\,\text{keV}$ $^{55}\text{Mn}$ bounds are much more robust to stellar modeling uncertainties.
ai.summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) are hypothetical light pseudoscalar particles motivated by extensions of the Standard Model; if they couple to nucleons, hot stellar cores can thermally excite atomic nuclei that then de-excite by emitting mono-energetic ALPs instead of photons. While previous stellar searches focused on the $14.4\,\text{keV}$ transition of $^{57}\text{Fe}$ (which has an odd number of neutrons and mainly probes ALP-neutron couplings), the authors model the red supergiant Betelgeuse using the MESA stellar evolution code to study higher-energy transitions in odd-proton nuclei: $^{55}\text{Mn}$ ($125.9\,\text{keV}$) and $^{23}\text{Na}$ ($440.2\,\text{keV}$). As these ALPs travel toward Earth, ultralight ones can convert into X-ray/gamma-ray photons inside the Galactic magnetic field ($a \to \gamma$), while heavier ones can decay in flight into photon pairs ($a \to \gamma\gamma$). By searching archival hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray observations of Betelgeuse from NuSTAR and INTEGRAL-ISGRI and finding no excess emission, the authors place new constraints on ALP-proton and ALP-photon interactions up to ALP masses of $440\,\text{keV}$.

papers.abstract: SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy. To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $\mu$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

conclusions: SIRMOS will survey the $\sim 14,000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ Euclid footprint over 3 years ($500\,\mathrm{Gpc}^3$ volume), using Euclid's near-IR imaging for target selection to obtain $\sim 10^8$ galaxy spectra at $1 < z < 4$.

By using a 2048$\times$1080 Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) as a reconfigurable electronic slitmask over a $0.9\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ field of view, the instrument can acquire up to 4,000 slit spectra simultaneously at spectral resolution $R=1300$.

This slit-based design achieves a redshift precision of $\sigma_z/(1+z) \simeq 10^{-4}$—an order of magnitude more accurate than the slitless grism spectroscopy of Euclid and Roman, which enables much sharper mapping of small-scale cosmic walls, voids, and redshift-space distortions.

Operating above the atmosphere provides continuous $1.25\text{--}2.5\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ wavelength coverage with no water-vapor absorption gaps or OH airglow noise, eliminating redshift-dependent selection biases to tightly constrain cosmic acceleration, primordial non-Gaussianity (inflation), and the sum of neutrino masses.

ai.summary: Mapping the 3D large-scale structure of galaxies at high redshifts ($1 < z < 4$) is crucial for testing cosmic acceleration, inflation, and neutrino masses, because key galaxy emission lines (like $\mathrm{H}\alpha$, $[\mathrm{O\,III}]$, and $[\mathrm{O\,II}]$) shift into the near-infrared (near-IR). From the ground, near-IR spectroscopy is severely hindered by atmospheric water-vapor absorption gaps and bright, time-varying hydroxyl (OH) airglow emission, while space missions like Euclid and Roman rely on "slitless" spectroscopy—dispersing light from the entire field at once, which suffers from overlapping spectra (source confusion) and degraded resolution for extended galaxies. This paper presents the technical concept for SIRMOS (Satellite for Infrared Multi-Object Spectroscopy), a proposed NASA Medium Explorer (MIDEX) mission featuring a 60 cm space telescope and a Digital Micromirror Device (DMD)—an array of tiny programmable mirrors that acts as a reconfigurable slitmask in space. By using Euclid's wide near-IR imaging catalog to select targets and flipping individual micromirrors to direct up to 4,000 galaxies at a time into a spectrograph, SIRMOS plans to measure 100 million high-precision redshifts across the $14,000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ Euclid Wide Survey footprint without atmospheric gaps or slitless confusion.

papers.title: Derivation of OH sum rules without Rayleigh--Jeans approximation: a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants
papers.authors: Renzhi Su, Minfeng Gu
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that the optical depths of any OH $\Lambda$-doublet quartet obey one exact linear relation in every velocity channel. No approximation is needed. The only exception is the $^{2}\Pi_{1/2}$ $J{=}1/2$ level, which has three transitions only, because its $F{=}0{\leftrightarrow}0$ line is strictly forbidden. The relation is $\tau_{S_1}(v)/\mu_{S_1}^{2}+\tau_{S_2}(v)/\mu_{S_2}^{2}=\tau_{M_1}(v)/(a\mu_{M_1}^{2})+\tau_{M_2}(v)/(b\mu_{M_2}^{2})$, where $a=2J^{2}+J-1$, $b=2J^{2}+3J$, and the $\mu_i^{2}$ are reduced transition dipole moments derived from the catalogued Einstein $A$ coefficients. It holds equally for gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), for non-LTE gas, for masers and for conjugate gas. We suggest that it is a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants.

conclusions: For any OH $\Lambda$-doublet quartet with rotational quantum number $J > 1/2$, the optical depths in each velocity channel $v$ obey the exact linear relation $\tau_{S_1}(v)/\mu_{S_1}^2 + \tau_{S_2}(v)/\mu_{S_2}^2 = \tau_{M_1}(v)/(a\mu_{M_1}^2) + \tau_{M_2}(v)/(b\mu_{M_2}^2)$, where $a = 2J^2 + J - 1$ and $b = 2J^2 + 3J$. For the 18 cm ground state ($J=3/2$), assuming equal dipole moments $\mu_i$ recovers $\tau_{1612} + \tau_{1720} = \tau_{1665}/5 + \tau_{1667}/9$.

Because the sum rule follows purely from level population algebra and angular-momentum coupling (with no Rayleigh–Jeans or LTE assumptions), it holds identically for absorbing gas, non-LTE environments, masers, and low-$T_{\rm ex}$ conjugate satellite lines, failing only for the 4.7 GHz ($J=1/2$) band where the $F=0 \leftrightarrow 0$ transition is strictly forbidden ($a=0$).

For far-infrared-pumped 18 cm conjugate satellite lines, the anomalous optical depths cancel ($\tau_{S_1}^{\rm an}/\mu_{S_1}^2 = -\tau_{S_2}^{\rm an}/\mu_{S_2}^2$), but total satellite optical depths only sum to zero when the underlying thermal population difference is negligible.

Applying the sum rule channel-by-channel in velocity space avoids systematic uncertainties from fitting multi-component non-Gaussian line profiles and allows radio-frequency interference (RFI)-contaminated channels to be cleanly excised in upcoming SKA surveys.
