Because the frequencies of these four lines depend differently on fundamental constants like the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ and the proton-to-electron mass ratio $m_p/m_e$, comparing their velocity profiles across cosmic time is a classic probe of whether fundamental constants evolve. In this paper, the authors use pure level-population algebra and angular-momentum coupling rules to derive an exact linear relation ("sum rule") connecting the optical depths $\tau(v)$ of the चार lines in every velocity channel, completely bypassing the high-temperature Rayleigh–Jeans approximation ($kT_{\rm ex} \gg h\nu$) and local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumptions required in previous derivations. This makes the relation valid even in extreme non-LTE regimes like astrophysical masers or "conjugate" satellite lines (where far-infrared pumping drives one satellite line into emission and the other into absorption with very low excitation temperatures), allowing upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA) surveys to test fundamental constant variations channel-by-channel without needing to fit complex, blended Gaussian line shapes.

papers.title: Can inflationary axion fluctuations dominate over misalignment?
papers.authors: Seung J. Lee, Sarunas Verner, Bingrong Yu
papers.abstract: The relic abundance of light stable axion dark matter is usually set by misalignment. We study whether the inflationary fluctuations of the axion can dominate instead, and we follow the modes analytically through an instantaneous transition from de Sitter expansion to radiation domination, neglecting the axion mass during inflation and keeping it afterward. Since the energy density is quadratic in the field, a fluctuation-dominated abundance carries an isocurvature perturbation even when the mean displacement vanishes. For a canonical minimally coupled axion the spectrum is scale invariant, and fluctuation-dominated dark matter exceeds the Planck isocurvature limit by about eight orders of magnitude. An inflaton-dependent kinetic function or a nonminimal coupling to the Ricci scalar tilts the spectrum blue, moving the fluctuation power from CMB scales to small scales. Imposing the Planck limit at the pivot scale, we find that fluctuation-dominated dark matter with a constant kinetic slope requires the spectral tilt $n_\eta-1\gtrsim0.27$ and the axion mass $m_{\eta} \gtrsim200 \rm{GeV}$ at $H_I=10^{10}\rm{GeV}$, and $n_\eta-1\gtrsim0.34$ and $m_\eta\gtrsim4.5\,$keV at $H_I=10^{13}\rm{GeV}$. A kinetic function with a running slope lowers these masses to $1.4~\rm{GeV}$ and $0.7\,$eV, respectively. For the QCD axion, whose oscillations start late, we estimate that any single power-law spectrum blue enough to satisfy the pivot limit gives too little fluctuation abundance, and misalignment dominates.

conclusions: For a canonical, minimally coupled axion, setting the dark matter abundance purely via inflationary fluctuations yields a scale-invariant spectrum whose quadratic density perturbations exceed the Planck isocurvature limit by 8 to 9 orders of magnitude.

To evade CMB bounds via a constant blue spectral tilt (from a linear exponential kinetic function or a positive Ricci curvature coupling), the spectrum must satisfy $n_\eta - 1 \gtrsim 0.27$ with an axion mass $m_\eta \gtrsim 200\,\mathrm{GeV}$ at $H_I = 10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ (or $n_\eta - 1 \gtrsim 0.34$ and $m_\eta \gtrsim 4.5\,\mathrm{keV}$ at $H_I = 10^{13}\,\mathrm{GeV}$), meaning only relatively heavy axion-like particles can be produced this way.

Introducing a running spectral tilt (via a quadratic exponential kinetic coupling) makes the spectrum strongly blue on CMB scales while flattening on smaller scales where the relic abundance is set, relaxing the minimum axion mass down to $1.4\,\mathrm{GeV}$ at $H_I = 10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}$, $0.7\,\mathrm{eV}$ at $H_I = 10^{13}\,\mathrm{GeV}$, and $\sim 0.01\,\mathrm{eV}$ near the tensor bound ($H_I = 4.7 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{GeV}$).

For the standard QCD axion, whose oscillations begin late ($T \sim 1\,\mathrm{GeV}$), any single power-law spectrum blue enough to satisfy the Planck isocurvature bound leaves too little fluctuation power to make up the dark matter, ensuring that conventional misalignment dominates.
ai.summary: Axion dark matter is traditionally thought to be produced via the "misalignment mechanism," where a uniform background axion field is held frozen by early-universe expansion until the Hubble rate drops below the axion mass, at which point it oscillates and behaves like cold dark matter. However, during inflation, the axion also acquires quantum fluctuations across different spatial scales; this paper investigates whether the energy stored in these fluctuations can dominate the dark matter relic abundance instead of the homogeneous misalignment background. Because the axion energy density is proportional to the square of the field, a fluctuation-dominated dark matter component inevitably generates "isocurvature" perturbations (fluctuations in the local ratio of dark matter to radiation) even when the mean background field is zero, which are tightly constrained by Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations. By analytically tracking the axion modes from inflation into the radiation-dominated era, the authors show that a standard axion violates Planck CMB isocurvature limits by 8–9 orders of magnitude, and can only survive if non-minimal couplings (to the inflaton via a kinetic function or to the spacetime Ricci curvature $R$) tilt the fluctuation spectrum strongly "blue" to shift power away from large CMB scales onto small scales.

papers.title: Dark Matter Coherent Freeze-Out Mechanism: A Comprehensive Analysis
papers.authors: Steven Ferrante, Lillian Luo, Maxim Perelstein, Bingrong Yu
papers.abstract: Both Weakly-Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) and Axion-Like Particle (ALP) are attractive particle dark matter candidates. In this paper we consider a scenario in which both WIMP and ALP are present. The two species interact via a non-derivative quadratic coupling modeled on the axion-nucleon interaction in QCD. We show that even a small (Planck-suppressed) coupling can drastically modify the cosmological history of both species. In the very early Universe, the ALP field acquires a vacuum expectation value, and the system undergoes an inverse phase transition at a temperature around or below the weak scale. WIMPs may remain in equilibrium far beyond the usual freeze-out time, eventually decoupling via a novel "coherent freeze-out" mechanism. WIMP annihilation cross sections several orders of magnitude above the canonical thermal target value can be consistent with the observed relic density in the coherent freeze-out scenario. At the same time, coherent oscillations of the ALP field do not begin until after the phase transition, and the initial conditions for these oscillations are set by the thermal physics of the phase transition. The ALP relic density is then predicted unambiguously in terms of the WIMP mass and coupling. We term this scenario "ALP miracle", since the observed relic density is obtained when these parameters are around their natural values, the weak and the Planck scale. The ALP miracle scenario prefers the ALP mass above about $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}$, far larger than other popular ALP dark matter models. The ALP miracle parameter space overlaps with a currently allowed region of the QCD axion band, a large fraction of which is expected to be probed by the proposed IAXO experiment.

conclusions: In the first-order phase transition regime ($\kappa < \kappa_c \approx 0.2$), WIMPs undergo "coherent freeze-out" at inverse temperatures $x_{\rm cfo} \approx 0.836\,\kappa^{-1/3} \gg 25$, allowing WIMP annihilation cross sections up to six orders of magnitude above the canonical thermal value (in the vacuum-dominated inflating regime, $\kappa \lesssim 5\times 10^{-9}$) to reproduce the observed relic density.

In the crossover regime ($\kappa > 0.2$), thermal dynamics erase the dependence on arbitrary inflationary initial conditions and set the ALP oscillation amplitude directly; this "ALP miracle" naturally yields the observed dark matter abundance for weak-scale WIMP masses and Planck-scale couplings ($\Lambda \sim M_{\rm Pl}$).

The ALP miracle scenario requires relatively heavy ALP masses ($m_\phi \gtrsim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}$), overlapping with a viable region of the canonical QCD axion band that will be largely tested by the upcoming IAXO helioscope experiment.

Although the first-order phase transition regime experiences strong supercooling before bubble nucleation occurs near $x_{\rm cfo}$, the transition completes too rapidly to generate an observable gravitational-wave background.
ai.summary: Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs, heavy thermal relics near the electroweak scale) and Axion-Like Particles (ALPs, light classical scalar fields typically produced non-thermally via coherent field oscillations) are usually treated as separate dark matter paradigms. In this paper, the authors study the early-Universe thermodynamics when both species coexist and interact via a tiny, Planck-suppressed quadratic coupling ($\bar{\chi}\chi\phi^2/\Lambda$) modeled on the QCD axion-nucleon interaction. Through one-loop finite-temperature potential calculations and coupled field/Boltzmann equations, they show that coherent forward scattering off the hot WIMP plasma gives the ALP a non-zero vacuum expectation value at high temperatures, which lowers the effective WIMP mass and keeps WIMPs relativistic far longer than usual. As the Universe cools, the bare ALP mass restores symmetry in an "inverse phase transition" (either a first-order transition or a smooth crossover), suddenly restoring the bare WIMP mass to trigger a delayed "coherent freeze-out" while simultaneously setting fixed, predictive initial conditions for ALP oscillations.

papers.title: Prospects for Near-Far Constraints on Reionization from Simulated LSST Observations of Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies and Stellar Streams
papers.authors: Aritra Kundu, Robyn Sanderson, Nora Shipp, Adrien Thob, Adam Lidz, Nondh Panithanpaisal
papers.abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will detect resolved stellar populations of intact dwarf galaxies and disrupted stellar streams in the Milky Way (MW) halo and beyond, opening a new avenue for near-field cosmology, particularly for constraining the faint galaxies during reionization. To interpret these data, we present and publicly release mock LSST catalogs of satellites, stellar streams, phase-mixed galaxies, and field galaxies around 13 MW-mass hosts in the FIRE-2 zoom-in simulations, generated with \textsf{py-ananke}. Using a surface brightness limit of $\mu_{g} \leq 34$ $\rm{mag}$ $\rm{arcsec^{-2}}$, we find that $\approx29\%$ of streams with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 5 \times 10^5$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable with tidal tails, while another $\approx38\%$ are detectable only through their bound progenitors and would appear as satellites. We estimate that $\approx96\%$ of satellites and $\approx64\%$ of field galaxies (out to $\sim$3.5 Mpc) with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable, decreasing to $\approx$59\% and $\approx$42\% for $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{4.5}$ $M_{\odot}$ owing to resolution limits. Including streams detectable as satellites reproduces the radial distribution of observed MW satellites, suggesting that some observed satellites may be bound remnants of disrupted systems. Our mock galaxies match the sizes of observed satellites with $M_{\rm{V}} \lesssim -6$. Star-formation histories computed from only the detectable stars broadly recover the simulated star-formation histories. As an application, we test the near-far technique for reconstructing the proto-MW ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) during reionization ($z \gtrsim 6$). Adding the detectable streams improves the recovered faint-end slope at $z = 7$ and reduces the halo-to-halo scatter by $\approx33\%$.

conclusions: For an LSST surface brightness limit of $\mu_g \leq 34\text{ mag arcsec}^{-2}$ and 1-year magnitude depths, $\approx 29\%$ of simulated stellar streams ($M_\star \gtrsim 5 \times 10^5\,M_\odot$) have detectable tidal tails, while another $\approx 38\%$ are only detectable via their bound core remnants and would be misclassified as intact satellites.

For stellar masses $M_\star \gtrsim 10^5\,M_\odot$, LSST will detect $\approx 96\%$ of intact satellites, $\approx 95\%$ of bound stream progenitors, and $\approx 64\%$ of local field galaxies out to $\sim 3.5\text{ Mpc}$.

Including streams whose bound cores are detected as satellites brings the simulated radial distribution of satellites into good agreement with Milky Way observations, suggesting some known Milky Way satellites are actually bound remnants of tidally disrupted systems.

Adding detectable streams and stream progenitors to intact galaxies when reconstructing the $z = 7$ proto-Milky Way UVLF increases the normalization around $M_{\rm UV} \sim -10$ by a factor of $\gtrsim 2$, halves the bias in the recovered faint-end slope (from $\approx 0.2$ to $\approx 0.1$), and reduces halo-to-halo scatter by $\approx 33\%$.
ai.summary: To understand what reionized the Universe at $z \gtrsim 6$, we need to know the abundance of ultra-faint early galaxies (the faint end of the ultraviolet luminosity function, or UVLF), many of which are too dim even for JWST to see directly. The "near-far" technique bypasses this limit by using resolved stars in present-day Milky Way dwarf galaxies as fossil records to reconstruct their star-formation histories and infer the brightness of their high-redshift progenitors—though past analyses have ignored early galaxies that were tidally shredded into stellar streams by the Milky Way. In this paper, the authors use `py-ananke` to generate public mock Vera C. Rubin Observatory (LSST) star catalogs from 13 Milky Way-mass zoom-in hydrodynamical simulations in the FIRE-2 suite, evaluating which intact dwarf galaxies and disrupted stellar streams LSST will actually detect. They show that folding LSST-detectable stellar streams and partially stripped stream remnants into the near-far analysis recovers a much more accurate and less noisy census of reionization-era galaxies.

papers.title: Late reheating in the era of precision cosmology
papers.authors: Kensuke Akita, Oleksii Ihnatenko, Maksym Ovchynnikov
papers.abstract: We study the minimum cosmic reheating temperature allowed by recent measurements of primordial nuclear abundances and of the cosmic microwave background. We find that reheating by decays of a light particle into electrons and neutrinos is compatible with both at temperatures around 0.4 MeV, an order of magnitude below the bound for purely electromagnetic channels. This scenario has implications for cosmology and laboratory searches. For example, nearly standard neutrino radiation can coexist with a smaller active neutrino mass density at unchanged physical masses, by up to a factor of five for normal ordering. The weaker suppression of clustering changes matter power at the percent level, which forthcoming galaxy surveys and lensing measurements may probe. Late reheating also suppresses sterile neutrino production at mixings within the projected reach of laboratory experiments.

conclusions: Allowing a scalar reheater ($m_X \sim 5\text{--}10\,\text{MeV}$) to undergo mixed decays into both $e^+e^-$ and unequally weighted neutrino flavors lowers the minimum viable cosmic reheating temperature to $T_{\text{RH}} \simeq 0.4\,\text{MeV}$—an order of magnitude below the $\sim 5\text{--}6\,\text{MeV}$ limit for purely electromagnetic decays.

Because injected neutrinos carry higher average momenta than a standard Fermi–Dirac bath, the model reproduces a near-standard $N_{\text{eff}} \simeq 2.89$ with fewer total particles; for normal ordering, this depletes the heaviest mass eigenstate and reduces the late-time physical neutrino mass density by a factor of $3$ to $5$ at fixed $\sum m_\nu \simeq 0.06\,\text{eV}$.

This reduced late-time neutrino mass density weakens free-streaming suppression, boosting the $z=0$ linear matter power spectrum by $\sim 1\%$ at $k = 0.1\text{--}1\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ and making a true mass sum of $0.059\,\text{eV}$ mimic a thermal relic sum of $\sum m_\nu \simeq 0.019\,\text{eV}$—offering a mechanism to reconcile oscillation bounds with tight CMB+DESI upper limits.

Late mixed reheating around $T_{\text{RH}} \simeq 1\,\text{MeV}$ with zero branching to $\nu_\mu$ suppresses the thermal production of $\sim 23\,\text{eV}$ sterile neutrinos by a factor of $\simeq 40$ compared to $5\,\text{MeV}$ instantaneous reheating, bringing large active-sterile mixings ($|U_{\mu 4}|^2 \sim 10^{-3}\text{--}10^{-2}$) within the reach of laboratory experiments (SHiP, nuSCOPE) without violating hot dark matter bounds.

ai.summary: Cosmic reheating—the process that populates the hot thermal plasma after inflation or a period of early matter domination—must occur early enough not to spoil Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) or the cosmic microwave background (CMB). If a long-lived scalar particle reheats the universe solely via electromagnetic decays near the MeV scale, weak interactions are too slow to thermalize neutrinos, lowering the effective number of relativistic species ($N_{\text{eff}}$) and altering the neutron-to-proton ratio, which restricts the reheating temperature to $T_{\text{RH}} \gtrsim 5\text{--}6\,\text{MeV}$. In this paper, the authors use a Monte Carlo neutrino transport code ($\nu\text{DSMC}$) coupled to a BBN network (`PRIMAT`) and the `CLASS` Boltzmann solver to study "mixed decays," where a light scalar ($m_X \sim \text{few}\text{--}10\,\text{MeV}$) decays directly into both $e^+e^-$ pairs and different active neutrino flavors. They show that tuning the branching fractions across neutrino flavors simultaneously preserves standard $N_{\text{eff}}$ and primordial helium/deuterium abundances while producing a hotter, sparser relic neutrino population, which significantly lowers the late-time neutrino mass density and reduces neutrino free-streaming suppression of the matter power spectrum.

papers.title: Fresh Look at Shift Symmetric Modified Gravity
papers.authors: Rodrigo Calderon, Eric V. Linder
papers.abstract: Shift symmetric Horndeski gravity can be a simple, well posed theory with protection against quantum corrections. Overturning conventional thought that such a theory cannot cross the phantom divide ($w=-1$) we present both analytic and numerical proof that it can. We carry out a detailed dynamical systems analysis showing the evolution of ghost free and stable regions within the model family, identify the fixed point and dynamical attractor structure, and derive the interaction of the $w=-1$ curve with these phase space structures. This reveals two mechanisms for cosmologies crossing the phantom divide while preserving shift symmetry.

conclusions: For monomial kinetic ($K \sim X^n$) and braiding ($G_3 \sim X^m$) terms with $m=(2n-1)/4$, healthy trajectories linking an early matter-dominated era to a future de Sitter attractor exist for $0 < n < 1/2$ (giving a phantom early equation of state $w = 1/(2n-1) < -1$), whereas $n < 0$ introduces ghosts and $n > 1/2$ spoils early matter domination.

In the 2D phase space of dimensionless kinetic and braiding density fractions $(x_k, x_g)$, the phantom divide $w = -1$ forms a parabola $Q(x_k, x_g) = x_g^2 + 2n x_g + 8n^2 x_k = 0$; previous no-go arguments assumed zero conserved shift-charge ($C = 0$), which restricts trajectories to the straight line $x_g = -2n x_k$ that can only touch the parabola at the fixed points rather than cross it.

A constant-exponent model with $1/2 < n \le 1$ (demonstrated for $n = 3/4$) can cross $w = -1$ from above without ghosts or instabilities if initialized near the braiding-dominated fixed point, though this lacks a viable matter-dominated era.

Allowing the kinetic exponent $n(X) \equiv d\ln K / d\ln X$ to transition smoothly via a sigmoid from $n_{\rm early} = 0.35$ to $n_{\rm late} = 0.05$ rotates the $w = -1$ parabola in phase space, enabling a completely healthy cosmology with standard early matter domination that crosses from $w < -1$ to $w > -1$ (and back again).

ai.summary: Recent cosmological data (such as DESI BAO) hint that dark energy's equation of state $w$ may evolve across the "phantom divide" ($w = -1$), a transition that standard single-field quintessence cannot make without developing fatal ghost or gradient instabilities. While Horndeski scalar-tensor gravity can cross $w = -1$, theorists strongly prefer "shift-symmetric" models—where the Lagrangian depends only on derivatives of the scalar field ($X = \frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^2$) via kinetic $K(X)$ and kinetic-braiding $G_3(X)\Box\phi$ terms—because shift symmetry protects the theory against high-energy quantum loop corrections; however, conventional wisdom held that unbroken shift-symmetric Horndeski theories cannot stably cross $w = -1$. Calderón and Linder overturn this no-go lore by performing an exact 2D dynamical systems phase-space analysis of shift-symmetric Horndeski gravity with zero potential and luminal gravitational wave speed. They prove both analytically and numerically that the $w = -1$ boundary is a parabola in phase space that acts as a traversable one-way door when the conserved shift-symmetry charge is non-zero, identifying two concrete mechanisms that achieve a completely healthy, ghost-free phantom crossing.

papers.title: Axionic Quintessence in Heterotic String Theory
papers.authors: David Andriot, Margherita Putti, Leo Veissiere
papers.abstract: We investigate axionic quintessence in heterotic string compactifications. Starting from the ten-dimensional theory, we derive the four-dimensional axion effective action, including gauge couplings and non-perturbative potentials, and identify the curvature terms that can correct it. We examine the geometric requirements for ultralight axions generated by exponentially suppressed worldsheet instantons, finding significant restrictions through an exploratory scan of toric Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces. In an illustrative K3-fibred setup, the minimal benchmark also encounters a tension with the positivity of the one-loop corrected gauge kinetic functions. Aligned worldsheet-instanton contributions provide a way to alleviate this tension and yield an ultralight axion with a phenomenologically relevant decay constant. Our analysis also identifies lower-action instantons whose contributions must be controlled to preserve the ultralight axion. We then study the resulting class of quintessence potentials and qualitatively compare their late-time cosmological solutions with observationally preferred ranges.

conclusions: A minimal heterotic setup relying on a single large two-cycle fails a scan over toric Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces when simultaneously imposing perturbatively controlled string volumes ($\mathcal{V} \le 25$) and positive one-loop corrected gauge kinetic functions.

Using "aligned" worldsheet instanton charge vectors in a three-modulus K3-fibred benchmark resolves these geometric and gauge tensions, yielding an ultralight quintessence axion with an effective decay constant $f \simeq 0.4\,M_{\mathrm{p}}$ and a realistic visible-sector gauge coupling ($\alpha_{\mathrm{YM}} \simeq 1/25$).

In a separate audit of 55 aligned geometric candidates, every geometry exhibited lower-action instantons that would spoil the ultralight axion mass unless their prefactors are suppressed by gauge-bundle zero modes or exact cancellations—showing that geometry alone is insufficient to guarantee a viable potential.

Assuming such bundle suppression holds, the resulting thawing quintessence models ("Axionic" $V \propto 1 + \cos(\phi/f)$ and "Hilltop-like" $V \propto \cos(\phi/f)$) produce a late-time evolving dark energy equation of state $w_\phi(z)$ qualitatively compatible with recent DESI preferences for dynamical dark energy ($3.0\text{--}3.5\,\sigma$ over $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$).
ai.relevance_reason: While the paper touches on thawing quintessence and DESI dynamical dark energy constraints (a medium-relevance topic), its core focus is formal 10D heterotic string compactifications, Calabi-Yau geometry, and worldsheet instantons rather than large-scale structure simulations, emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Recent DESI and supernova measurements have hinted that dark energy may be dynamical rather than a pure cosmological constant, reviving interest in quintessence—a light scalar field rolling slowly down a potential at late times. Axions (pseudo-scalar fields with a shift symmetry that protects their tiny masses from quantum corrections) are prime candidates for quintessence and arise naturally when extra dimensions are compactified in string theory, though most prior work has focused on Type II string theory rather than the heterotic string. Here, the authors derive a 4D effective theory of axions starting from 10D $E_8 \times E_8$ heterotic string theory compactified on a 6D Calabi-Yau manifold, tracking higher-derivative curvature corrections, one-loop gauge couplings, and non-perturbative "worldsheet instantons" (strings wrapping internal 2D surfaces that generate periodic cosine potentials). They test whether these compactifications can simultaneously produce an ultralight axion at the dark energy scale and a near-Planckian decay constant $f$ (needed for slow roll) without breaking geometric control or ruining the Standard Model gauge coupling, and then compare the resulting "thawing" cosine potentials to DESI late-time expansion constraints.

papers.title: CROMA: a GPU-accelerated Fokker--Planck solver for modeling non-thermal emission in post-processing cosmological simulations
papers.authors: Kosuke Nishiwaki, Claudio Gheller, Gianfranco Brunetti, Katsuaki Asano
papers.abstract: Numerical modeling of cosmic-ray (CR) spectra and the resulting non-thermal emission is important for understanding the physical mechanisms of CR acceleration and transport in astrophysical environments. Galaxy clusters and cosmic filaments provide particularly important environments for studying these processes, where shocks, turbulence, magnetic fields, and CRs jointly shape diffuse synchrotron emission. Spectrally resolved modeling of CRs, including cooling, re-acceleration, and hadronic interactions, requires solving time-dependent Fokker--Planck (FP) equations. An increasing number of studies employ FP solvers coupled with magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations to follow the evolution of CRs in dynamically evolving environments. We present a new C/C++-based FP solver with GPU acceleration for post-processing outputs from cosmological MHD simulations. The code evolves CR proton and electron spectra along Lagrangian tracer trajectories and consistently includes re-acceleration and secondary-particle production processes. With the Chang--Cooper finite-difference scheme, the FP equation for each tracer is reduced to an independent tridiagonal system, which is solved on NVIDIA GPUs using a CUDA implementation of the parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) algorithm. The code uses sub-stepping between tracer snapshots, with the timestep constrained by the relevant CR cooling or re-acceleration timescale, and a batching algorithm that groups tracers with similar sub-stepping patterns for efficient execution. We find that the GPU acceleration increases the per-node throughput by a factor of $\approx$10 on the Leonardo Booster system operated by CINECA. The fast FP solver is useful for high-resolution simulations dedicated to comparison with next-generation radio observations and future multi-messenger applications combining radio, gamma-ray, and high-energy neutrino observations.

conclusions: Using four NVIDIA A100 GPUs on a Leonardo Booster node, the CUDA backend reaches a throughput of $\approx 1600$ tracers $\text{s}^{-1}$ compared to $\approx 120$ tracers $\text{s}^{-1}$ on 32 CPU cores, representing a $\sim 10\times$ per-node speedup that enables post-processing simulations down to several-kpc spatial resolution.

Precomputed lookup tables for pitch-angle-integrated synchrotron kernels accelerate the emissivity calculation by a factor of $\approx 10^3$ while keeping relative numerical errors below $\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})$ across the main frequency range.

An MPI load-balancing pre-pass that redistributes tracers based on their estimated total sub-steps adds only $\sim 0.3\text{ s}$ of overhead while eliminating workload imbalances of $\sim 7\%$ that would otherwise cost tens of seconds in GPU wall-time.
ai.summary: Galaxy clusters and cosmic filaments host diffuse radio emission (such as radio halos and relics) produced when relativistic cosmic-ray (CR) electrons spiral in magnetic fields and emit synchrotron radiation. Because the shocks and turbulence in the intra-cluster medium are too weak to accelerate thermal particles from scratch, accurately predicting this emission requires tracking how pre-existing cosmic rays cool, get stochastically re-accelerated by turbulence, and produce secondary particles via proton-proton collisions over cosmic time—governed in momentum space by the Fokker–Planck (FP) advection-diffusion PDE. The authors introduce CROMA, an open-source C/C++ and CUDA post-processing code that solves the time-dependent FP equation for CR protons and electrons along Lagrangian tracer particle trajectories extracted from cosmological magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations. By discretizing the momentum flux with a particle-conserving Chang–Cooper finite-difference scheme, grouping tracers with matching sub-step counts into batches, and solving the resulting tridiagonal matrix systems in parallel on GPUs using the parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) algorithm, CROMA makes high-resolution synthetic radio, gamma-ray, and neutrino maps computationally tractable for next-generation surveys like the SKA.

papers.title: A gaussian-process reconstruction of gravitational-wave friction from dark standard sirens
papers.authors: Michele Mancarella, Viola De Renzis, Alessandro Agapito
papers.abstract: Standard sirens provide a direct probe of the cosmic distance-redshift relation and therefore a powerful test of whether gravitational waves (GWs) propagate as predicted by general relativity on cosmological scales. In many extensions of general relativity, GW propagation is modified by an anomalous friction term, which alters the amplitude evolution and leads to a GW luminosity distance that differs from its electromagnetic counterpart. In this work, we develop a non-parametric reconstruction of this anomalous friction from dark standard sirens. We reconstruct its redshift dependence, encoded in the friction function $\alpha_M(z)$, with a Gaussian process (GP) and derive the corresponding GW-to-EM luminosity-distance ratio $\Xi(z)$ by integration, explicitly retaining the relation between the local friction modification and its accumulated effect on the observed distance, while enforcing a monotonic and invertible GW luminosity distance. We apply the method to the GWTC-5.0 catalog, jointly inferring the source population, modified propagation, and background cosmological parameters. We find no evidence for departures from GR, with $\alpha_M=0$ and $\Xi=1$ consistent with the posterior over the redshift range probed by the catalog. The result is stable under variations of the GP kernel, smoothness and amplitude priors, resolution prescription, and likelihood treatment. We further introduce function-space diagnostics for comparing flexible and parametric reconstructions, including prior calibration, prior-to-posterior contraction, common summaries of propagation-population degeneracies, and principal-component analysis. These tools make explicit which features are informed by the data and which are imposed by the function-space prior, providing a framework for interpretable non-parametric tests of gravitational-wave propagation.

conclusions: Applying the non-parametric GP reconstruction to the GWTC-5.0 BBH catalog—jointly fitting 235 parameters covering background cosmology ($H_0, \Omega_m, w_0$), BBH mass/merger-rate distributions, and GP nodes—yields no evidence for modified gravity, with $\alpha_M(z)=0$ and $\Xi(z)=1$ fully consistent with the posterior across the probed redshift range.

While local variations in the friction function $\alpha_M(z)$ show expected sensitivity to GP kernel choices and smoothness priors, the integrated distance ratio $\Xi(z)$ remains remarkably stable across all prior and likelihood variations.

Validation on 3000 simulated O5-like events demonstrates that the GR-centered GP prior accurately recovers both fiducial $\Lambda$CDM and extreme modified-gravity trajectories (such as non-monotonic DHOST models with $\Xi_0=1.8, n=3$) that standard two-parameter $(\Xi_0, n)$ models fail to capture.

Function-space diagnostics and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveal that while the degeneracy between modified GW propagation and the BBH merger rate evolution persists in non-parametric fits, the GP spreads posterior uncertainty across multiple independent redshift modes rather than artificially forcing it into a single coherent trajectory like the $(\Xi_0, n)$ ansatz.
ai.relevance_reason: While this paper tests modified gravity on cosmological scales ( specifically the Horndeski Planck-mass running $\alpha_M$), it focuses entirely on gravitational-wave standard sirens rather than large-scale structure simulations, emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In many modified gravity theories (such as Horndeski gravity with a time-varying effective Planck mass), gravitational waves (GWs) experience an anomalous "friction" $\alpha_M(z)$ as they travel across cosmic history, causing the luminosity distance inferred from GW amplitudes ($d_L^{\rm GW}$) to diverge from the standard electromagnetic luminosity distance ($d_L^{\rm EM}$). This effect can be tested using "dark standard sirens" (or spectral sirens)—merging binary black holes without electromagnetic counterparts whose redshifts are inferred statistically from features like peaks and cutoffs in the source-frame black hole mass distribution. Rather than relying on rigid two-parameter functional forms for the distance ratio $\Xi(z) \equiv d_L^{\rm GW}(z)/d_L^{\rm EM}(z)$, the authors develop a flexible Gaussian Process (GP) framework that directly reconstructs the local friction $\alpha_M(z)$ while strictly enforcing a monotonic, invertible GW distance-redshift relation and adapting its correlation length to the catalog's redshift resolution. They apply this hierarchical Bayesian pipeline to the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA GWTC-5.0 catalog—jointly inferring background $w_0$CDM cosmology, black hole population hyperparameters, and the GP propagation history—and introduce function-space diagnostics to disentangle true data constraints from prior assumptions.

papers.title: Phase-Twist Instability in a Coprecessing Neutrino Plasma
papers.authors: Damiano F. G. Fiorillo, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, Basudeb Dasgupta, Georg G. Raffelt
papers.abstract: Dense neutrino plasmas support collective flavor motion. We derive the first explicit dispersion relation about a flavor-nondiagonal background, focusing on the coprecession solution underlying spectral-split formation during the prompt neutrino burst of an electron-capture supernova. We show that slow phase modulations are unstable Goldstone modes, causing the coprecession plane to wobble with increasing amplitude. The instability emerges in the hydrodynamic limit, governed by conservation laws and without resolving flavor-precession resonances. Coprecessing neutrino plasmas resemble magnetized plasmas: a coherent flavor field drives flavor isospins to precess, and the phase-twist instability is the flavor analog of the firehose instability.

conclusions: "One-sided flavor coprecession states maximize the corotating flavor energy $\\mathcal{H}_0$ and are therefore strictly stable against homogeneous ($k = 0$) perturbations, which must conserve energy."

"Slow, spatially varying phase twists ($\\delta\\Phi \\propto e^{-i\\omega t + ikz}$) do not conserve refractive flavor energy and act as unstable Goldstone modes in the hydrodynamic limit, growing linearly with wavenumber: $\\gamma = \\mathrm{Im}(\\omega) \\propto k \\Delta v \\Delta\\theta$, where $\\Delta v$ is the velocity spread and $\\Delta\\theta$ is the angular spread of the flavor polarization vectors."

"At smaller spatial scales (larger $k$), perturbations resolve individual neutrino precession frequencies $|\\vec{H}_{\\mathbf{p}}|$ and enter the kinetic regime, where the instability turns over at $k \\sim |\\vec{H}_{\\mathbf{p}}|\\Delta\\theta/\\Delta v$ with a maximum growth rate $\\gamma_{\\mathrm{max}} \\sim |\\vec{H}_{\\mathbf{p}}|\\Delta\\theta^2$ before vanishing entirely."

"In this kinetic regime, wave-particle Cherenkov resonances ($\\omega - kv = 0$) from unmagnetized flavor-diagonal plasmas shift to cyclotron-like resonances ($\\omega - kv = \\pm|\\vec{H}_{\\mathbf{p}}|$), establishing a rigorous mathematical analogy between flavor-nondiagonal neutrino plasmas and magnetized electromagnetic plasmas."
ai.summary: In extremely dense environments like core-collapse supernovae and neutron-star mergers, neutrino–neutrino forward scattering creates a coherent weak potential that causes neutrino flavors to evolve collectively like a collisionless plasma. While most stability analyses study 'flavor-diagonal' backgrounds (where neutrinos start in pure flavor or mass eigenstates), the prompt electron-neutrino burst of a supernova naturally enters a 'coprecession' state—a flavor-nondiagonal configuration where the quantum flavor polarization vectors of different momentum modes lie in a common plane and rotate together around the mass axis. The authors derive the first explicit dispersion relation for perturbations around such a coprecessing background, combining an effective hydrodynamic theory at long wavelengths with a full linear-response kinetic theory at short wavelengths. They discover a generic 'phase-twist' instability: slow spatial modulations of the rotation phase act as unstable Goldstone modes that cause the coprecession plane to wobble and buckle, in exact analogy to the classic firehose instability of a magnetized plasma. This matters for supernova physics because this instability sets in before traditional 'spectral splits' (sharp swaps of flavor spectra across a critical energy) can finish forming.

papers.title: How particle physics stops ultra-relativistic bubbles and shapes their gravitational waves
papers.authors: Alessandro Strumia
papers.abstract: The gravitational-wave spectrum produced by ultra-relativistic bubbles in a first-order cosmological phase transition can be approximated in terms of their energy density as a function of bubble size. Bubble collisions and post-collision classical evolution negligibly change it. The dominant energy loss is particle scattering, often in the Landau--Pomeranchuk--Migdal regime. So the GW spectrum depends on the particle-physics coupling (interpolating between the `envelope' and `bulk flow' limits), on the interaction type (gauge, Yukawa, scalar quartic, ...), and on whether particle number is conserved. Finally, we consider broken global symmetries, which give a mixture of `elastic' and `inelastic' collisions.

conclusions: The gravitational-wave spectrum from colliding ultra-relativistic bubbles is determined almost entirely by how a bubble's wall energy density scales with its radius, whereas classical post-collision scalar field evolution negligibly alters the spectrum.

The dominant stopping mechanism for expanding bubble walls is quantum particle scattering in the Landau–Pomeranchuk–Migdal (LPM) regime (where multiple scatterings interfere destructively because the formation time of radiated particles exceeds the mean free path).

Varying the particle-physics coupling strength smoothly interpolates the resulting gravitational-wave spectrum between two standard analytical limits: the "envelope" approximation (where collided wall segments immediately lose energy) and the "bulk flow" model (where energy shells continue propagating freely after collision).

The spectral shape and peak scaling carry direct imprints of the underlying interaction type—distinguishing between gauge, Yukawa, and scalar quartic couplings, as well as whether particle number is conserved or broken global symmetries lead to mixed elastic and inelastic collisions.
ai.summary: In the early universe, a first-order cosmological phase transition proceeds through the nucleation and expansion of true-vacuum bubbles, whose collisions generate a stochastic background of gravitational waves (GWs). When these bubble walls accelerate to ultra-relativistic speeds, understanding how they transfer energy to the surrounding primordial plasma—and how they slow down after colliding—is essential for predicting the resulting GW spectrum. In this work, the author analytically models the energy loss of ultra-relativistic bubble walls by accounting for quantum particle scattering processes, particularly in the Landau–Pomeranchuk–Migdal (LPM) regime where high particle densities cause consecutive scatterings to interfere. By tying the GW spectrum directly to the energy density of the bubble walls as a function of their size, this framework demonstrates how microscopic particle physics properties—such as coupling strengths, interaction types, and symmetry breaking—directly shape macroscopic gravitational-wave observables.

papers.title: Asymmetric Reheating of a Dark Sector
papers.authors: Catarina Cosme, João G. Rosa, Inês Sequeira
papers.abstract: We study asymmetric post-inflationary reheating in a framework with two sequestered MSSM-like sectors (the ``visible'' and ``dark'' sectors) with different supersymmetry-breaking scales, with dark matter corresponding to the lightest dark baryons. In this setup, independent Affleck-Dine dynamics in the two sectors offers a natural explanation for the comparable abundances of visible and dark matter. We relate the resulting temperature hierarchy to the inflaton's partial decay widths in different kinematical regimes, where it may decay into dark sector particles via 2-, 3- or 4-body processes. The latter case yields the most asymmetric reheating scenario, and we discuss the implications of this regime for the dark sector's thermal history, namely regarding the corresponding strong and weak interactions. While in this kinematical regime the contribution of light dark sector degrees of freedom to $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ is negligible, we show that it increases significantly in the regime where 3-body decays are possible, particularly near the threshold for dark Higgs pair-production where $\Delta N_{\rm eff}^{\max} \simeq 0.078$. The current combined BBN+CMB+BAO bound leaves only a narrow allowed interval of the 2-body decay regime immediately above threshold, while next-generation CMB experiments could probe slightly below it.

conclusions: The ratio of dark-to-visible radiation energy densities after reheating is fixed directly by the ratio of the inflaton's partial decay widths, $\rho'/\rho = \Gamma'/\Gamma \equiv \epsilon$, which depends strongly on the inflaton-to-dark-Higgs mass ratio $m_\phi / M_{H'}$.

In the strongly hierarchical 4-body decay regime ($m_\phi < M_{H'}$), where both mediating dark Higgs bosons are virtual, the dark sector is so cold that it avoids a deconfined dark-QCD phase and contributes at most $\Delta N_{\rm eff} \simeq 3.3 \times 10^{-11}$ to dark radiation—completely invisible to current and planned cosmological surveys.

In the intermediate 3-body decay regime ($M_{H'} < m_\phi < 2M_{H'}$), the dark radiation contribution rises sharply as $m_\phi$ approaches the pair-production threshold, reaching $\Delta N_{\rm eff}^{\max} \simeq 0.078$ at $m_\phi = 2M_{H'}$ when accounting for finite-width effects.

Current combined BBN+CMB+BAO bounds rule out almost the entire on-shell 2-body regime ($m_\phi > 2M_{H'}$) except for a narrow window right above threshold ($m_\phi / M_{H'} \simeq 2.001$), while next-generation CMB experiments with sensitivity $\Delta N_{\rm eff} \simeq 0.06$ will be able to probe slightly below threshold ($m_\phi / M_{H'} \simeq 1.999$).
ai.summary: Today's energy density of dark matter is roughly five times that of ordinary baryons, raising the "coincidence problem" of why two seemingly unrelated components have such similar abundances. One solution is to imagine a hidden "dark sector" that mirrors the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM—a supersymmetric extension of particle physics) where matter-antimatter asymmetries are generated independently in both sectors after inflation via the Affleck–Dine mechanism (a process where oscillating scalar fields create net baryon number), but with a much higher supersymmetry-breaking mass scale in the dark sector. Because the dark scalar particles are much heavier than visible ones, the inflaton field decays into the dark sector much less efficiently during post-inflationary reheating, leaving the dark plasma significantly colder than the visible Universe. In this paper, the authors solve the coupled Boltzmann equations for this asymmetric reheating and compute the inflaton's decay rates across three kinematic regimes—4-body, 3-body, and 2-body decays—set by the ratio of the inflaton mass $m_\phi$ to the dark Higgs mass $M_{H'}$. They show how this mass hierarchy determines the dark sector's thermal history and its contribution to dark radiation ($\Delta N_{\rm eff}$, the effective number of extra relativistic neutrino species), pinpointing the narrow threshold window that upcoming CMB experiments can actually test.

papers.title: Unveiling the nonthermal environments of NGC 3411 and NGC 5903 through new MeerKAT observations
papers.authors: T. Pasini, F. De Gasperin, E. O'Sullivan, M. Brüggen, M. Gaspari, K. Kolokythas, E. Bulbul, E. Bahar
papers.abstract: Galaxy groups are key laboratories for investigating the interplay between active galactic nucleus (AGN) outbursts and the dynamical processes of the intra-group medium. We aim to characterize the morphology, spectral properties, and magnetic field structure of the diffuse nonthermal radio emission in two peculiar galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903, selected from an originally larger sample, in order to constrain its origin and its connection with the dynamics of the intra-group medium. We present new MeerKAT UHF- and L-band observations of the two groups, complemented by archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data already analyzed in previous works. In NGC 3411, we detect extended radio emission surrounding the central AGN over scales of ~70 kpc, and resolve previously undetected arc-shaped substructures on scales of ~20-30 kpc. This extended component exhibits a relatively uniform steep spectrum ($\alpha$ ~ -1.7). We discuss possible scenarios for its origin, including mini-halos, aged AGN plasma, weak shocks, and the possibility of a radio galaxy observed along the line of sight. In NGC 5903, MeerKAT reveals a complex filamentary morphology, including a previously unknown ring-like structure surrounding the central AGN. Spectral-index mapping shows localized flattening ($\alpha$ ~ -0.9) along the north arc, while polarization data reveal ordered magnetic fields and a patchy rotation measure distribution across the source. Together with the disturbed X-ray morphology, these results support a scenario in which fossil AGN plasma has been redistributed and locally reenergized by group-scale dynamical processes such as turbulence, shear, and weak compression. Our results demonstrate that galaxy groups can host a rich variety of nonthermal phenomena, whose properties can only be fully revealed through the combination of sensitive, high-resolution, and multifrequency radio observations.

conclusions: In NGC 3411, MeerKAT resolves ~20–30 kpc arc-shaped substructures within a ~70 kpc diffuse radio halo that exhibits a uniformly steep spectrum ($\alpha \simeq -1.7$, indicating aged, radiatively cooled electrons) and lacks a clear radio–X-ray surface-brightness correlation, disfavoring a standard cluster mini-halo origin.

The radio arcs in NGC 3411 likely trace fossil AGN plasma gently compressed and magnetically draped along a previously known X-ray "cool shell" interface (or potentially a radio galaxy viewed along the line of sight), rather than strong shock heating.

In the dynamically disturbed group NGC 5903, observations reveal a ~100 kpc filamentary radio structure and a previously unknown ~8 kpc ring around the central galaxy, with a mean spectral index of $\alpha \simeq -1.0$ that steepens to $\alpha < -1.5$ in the south and flattens locally to $\alpha \simeq -0.9$ along the northern arc.

Ordered magnetic field vectors aligned with the filaments and ring in NGC 5903 indicate that bulk intra-group "weather"—turbulence, shear, and weak adiabatic compression—is actively stretching and mildly re-accelerating fossil AGN electrons without requiring strong shocks.
ai.summary: In galaxy groups—bound systems smaller than massive clusters where most galaxies reside—energetic jets from central supermassive black holes (active galactic nuclei, or AGN) heat the surrounding hot, X-ray-emitting intra-group medium (IGrM) and prevent runaway cooling. Because this gas is faint, tracing how AGN energy couples to the group environment is difficult in X-rays alone, making diffuse synchrotron radio emission from relativistic "fossil" electrons (left over from past AGN outbursts) a vital tracer of gas dynamics. In this paper, the authors use high-resolution, multifrequency radio observations from the MeerKAT array (at ~815 MHz and ~1280 MHz), combined with archival Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray data, to map the radio morphology, spectral index $\alpha$ ($S_\nu \propto \nu^\alpha$, where steeper/more negative values indicate older, cooled plasma), and magnetic field polarization in two peculiar nearby galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903. They uncover intricate, previously unresolved arcs, rings, and filaments spanning tens of kiloparsecs in both systems, demonstrating that gentle group-scale "weather"—such as turbulence, shear, and magnetic draping—can redistribute and re-energize ancient AGN plasma without requiring strong shock waves.

papers.title: Primordial black holes from a type-IIB/F theory inflaton potential
papers.authors: Chitrak Sarkar, Amitava Choudhuri, Buddhadeb Ghosh
papers.abstract: We study the possibility of the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) using an inflaton potential constructed by stabilizing all Kähler moduli employing both the perturbative and non-perturbative corrections in the large volume scenario in type-IIB/F string theory. We further introduce a small perturbation in one of the Kähler moduli that modifies the existing potential in the field space. The effective correction in the moduli space is made by introducing a localised Gaussian bump, which induces an ultra-slow-roll feature in the inflaton potential during the early cosmological inflation. The evolution of the amplitude of the curvature power spectrum is solved numerically by using the Mukhanov-Sasaki equation, with Bunch-Davies initial conditions. The inclusion of the Gaussian bump produces a sustainable enhancement in the amplitude of curvature power spectra around $k\sim 1.12 \times 10^{9} Mpc^{-1}$ for the formation of PBHs. The abundance of PBHs ($f_{PBH}$) is calculated using the Press-Schechter formalism for different values of critical density contrast and presented in the background of contemporary $f_{PBH}$ bounds and checked for viability with existing microlensing bounds, corresponding to a mass value $10^{-6}M_\odot$ for $\delta$ threshold value $\delta_c=0.439$. The Hawking temperature and evaporation time are also determined for these black holes and found to be of the order of $2.78\times 10^{-15}$ GeV and $8.5\times10^{38}$ Gyr, respectively. The enhancement of curvature power spectra lies in the sensitivity region of the SKA observations, suggesting an indication that scalar-induced gravity waves may be probed in future observations.

conclusions: A localized Gaussian bump ($A \approx 4.58 \times 10^{-4}$, $\Delta = 10^{-2}$) added to the string-motivated Large Volume Scenario inflaton potential induces a transient ultra-slow-roll phase where the second slow-roll parameter reaches $\eta_i \approx 3$, amplifying the curvature power spectrum to $P_{\mathcal{R}}(k) \sim 10^{-2}$ at $k \sim 1.13 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$.

Upon horizon re-entry during radiation domination, these enhanced fluctuations form planetary-mass primordial black holes with $M_{\text{PBH}} \sim 10^{-6}\,M_\odot$; avoiding overproduction relative to current gravitational microlensing bounds requires a critical collapse density threshold of $\delta_c \ge 0.439$.

The resulting black holes have a negligible Hawking temperature ($\sim 2.78 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{GeV}$) and an evaporation lifetime ($\sim 8.5 \times 10^{38}\,\text{Gyr}$) vastly exceeding the age of the universe, making them stable dark matter candidates whose associated scalar-induced gravitational waves fall within the sensitivity band of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).
ai.summary: To form primordial black holes (PBHs) in the early universe, the primordial curvature power spectrum must be amplified by roughly seven orders of magnitude above its Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) value ($\sim 10^{-9}$ to $\sim 10^{-2}$) on small scales, which typically requires the inflaton field to temporarily enter an "ultra-slow-roll" (USR) phase on a nearly flat patch of its potential. In this paper, the authors start with an inflaton potential derived from type-IIB/F string theory (where scalar fields called Kähler moduli, which govern the size of compactified extra dimensions, are stabilized in the Large Volume Scenario) and argue that a small perturbation to the dynamical modulus manifests as a localized Gaussian bump in the potential. They numerically evolve quantum fluctuations across this bump using the exact Mukhanov-Sasaki equation—bypassing the standard slow-roll approximation, which breaks down during USR—and use the Press-Schechter formalism to compute the resulting PBH dark matter abundance. This provides a string-motivated toy model for generating planetary-mass PBH dark matter alongside second-order, scalar-induced gravitational waves that could be tested by future pulsar timing arrays.

papers.title: Rare Blue-core BCGs as Optical Signatures of ICM Cooling
papers.authors: M. Kluge, E. Bulbul, X. Zhang, M. McDonald, E. Artis, F. Balzer, R. Bender, Z. Ding, L. Fiorino, N. Malavasi, A. Merloni, T. Mistele, K. Nandra, M. Ramos-Ceja, M. Salvato, J. S. Sanders, S. Zelmer
papers.abstract: Blue cores in brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) trace recent central activity associated with cooling cluster atmospheres. We search for blue cores at $z<0.6$ in five eROSITA all-sky surveys using X-ray data, optical imaging, and optical spectroscopy. We identify 379 blue-core BCGs among 11352 systems (3.3%), although contamination increases toward higher redshift. Of these, 98 (0.86%) are X-ray bright. Their defining signature is a central $g-r$ color at least 0.2 mag bluer than the reference population within $a=20$ kpc before returning to the normal BCG envelope. Ha emission equivalent width correlates strongly with the blue continuum excess, consistent with young stellar components comprising ~0.1-1% of pre-existing stellar mass. Line ratios indicate widespread LINER-like excitation, with a larger star-forming contribution in blue Ha emitters but substantial non-stellar excitation. This activity is closely linked to the thermodynamics of the host-cluster gas. At $0.1R_{500}$, cooling times decrease from BCGs without significant Ha emission to red and then blue Ha emitters. Blue BCGs preferentially occur in clusters with $L_{\rm X,300}>10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$; red Ha emitters also favor higher X-ray luminosities. The blue-core fraction rises with optical richness. For systems with $t_{\rm cool}(0.1R_{500})<20$ Gyr, doubling richness increases the odds of hosting a blue-core BCG by $2.45\pm0.39$. This indicates that cluster scale carries information beyond cooling time, plausibly through the amount of gas available for cooling and condensation. The scarcity of blue BCGs without significant Ha emission disfavors isolated short bursts followed by long Ha-quiet fading phases. It can instead be explained by sustained or closely recurrent star formation over timescales much longer than 100 Myr, or by Ha persisting through additional excitation mechanisms as the young stellar component fades.

conclusions: Blue-core BCGs are rare: only 379 (3.3%) of the 11,352 clusters show a central $g-r$ color at least 0.2 mag bluer than normal within $a \lesssim 20\text{ kpc}$, and a high-purity X-ray-bright subset makes up just 0.86% (98 systems) of the full sample.

The blue continuum excess correlates strongly with $\text{H}\alpha$ emission-line strength and corresponds to a young stellar component comprising $\sim 0.1\text{--}1\%$ of the pre-existing galaxy stellar mass, though emission-line ratios show widespread non-stellar (LINER-like) excitation alongside star formation.

BCG activity tracks the thermodynamic state of the host cluster gas: X-ray cooling times at $0.1 R_{500}$ decrease progressively from passive BCGs to red $\text{H}\alpha$-emitting BCGs and finally to blue-core BCGs, which preferentially reside in X-ray luminous systems ($L_{\text{X},300} \gtrsim 10^{44}\text{ erg s}^{-1}$).

At fixed cooling time ($t_{\text{cool}}(0.1 R_{500}) < 20\text{ Gyr}$) and redshift, doubling the optical richness increases the odds of hosting a blue-core BCG by a factor of $2.45^{+0.39}_{-0.36}$, showing that a larger overall cluster gas reservoir promotes central star formation beyond the local cooling timescale alone.

Because blue-core BCGs without significant $\text{H}\alpha$ emission are extremely scarce, central star formation cannot be dominated by isolated short bursts followed by long $\text{H}\alpha$-quiet fading phases, instead requiring sustained/recurrent star formation over $\gg 100\text{ Myr}$ or persistent non-stellar $\text{H}\alpha$ excitation.
ai.summary: In relaxed galaxy clusters, the hot, X-ray-emitting intracluster medium (ICM) in the core can cool rapidly enough to condense onto the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG), overcoming active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback to trigger localized star formation. While most BCGs are old, red-and-dead elliptical galaxies, recent star formation leaves a visible signature as an anomalously blue core and optical emission lines like $\text{H}\alpha$. The authors combine X-ray data from five eROSITA all-sky surveys (eRASS:5) with DESI Legacy Surveys optical imaging and SDSS/DESI spectroscopy across 11,352 clusters at $z < 0.6$ to systematically census these rare blue-core BCGs. By linking radial optical color profiles and emission-line diagnostics to X-ray cooling times and cluster optical richness (a proxy for total cluster mass/scale), they show that central star formation depends not only on short local cooling times, but also on the total size of the cluster gas reservoir.

papers.title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
papers.authors: Qizhe Tang, Jingying Wang, Junhua Gu, Qian Zheng, Quan Guo, Tingyan Shen, Bixuan Zhao, Qiuyi Lai, Yan Huang, Kuanjun Li, Yang Feng
papers.abstract: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $\alpha=-0.825$ (where $S \propto \nu^{\alpha}$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

conclusions: Direction-dependent calibration and simulated primary-beam models improve the image dynamic range by a factor of 1.19–2.03 across the five frequency sub-bands compared to standard direction-independent calibration, substantially suppressing artefacts around ultra-bright sources like 3C 61.1.

The resulting 21CMA-DDR1 catalogue recovers 1246 extragalactic radio point sources within $5^\circ$ of the North Celestial Pole (an increase of $\sim 50\%$ over previous multi-day 21CMA catalogues) with angular resolution between 2.3 arcmin (at 100 MHz) and 1.4 arcmin (at 168.75 MHz).

In-band spectral fitting yields a median spectral index of $\alpha = -0.825$ ($S \propto \nu^\alpha$), which is physically consistent with synchrotron emission from extragalactic active galactic nuclei and star-forming galaxies.

Differential source counts at 150 MHz agree with existing surveys at the bright end, but exhibit a deficit below $S \lesssim 0.04\,\mathrm{Jy}$ due to thermal sensitivity limits and classical source confusion in a single 24-h integration.
ai.summary: Observing the redshifted 21-cm line from neutral hydrogen during the Epoch of Reionization ($z \approx 6\text{--}27$) is extremely challenging because foreground emission—from our Galaxy and extragalactic radio point sources—is four to five orders of magnitude brighter than the $\sim 10\text{--}30\,\mathrm{mK}$ cosmological signal. In radio interferometry, bright foreground sources also couple with varying ionospheric distortions and complex antenna beam patterns across the field of view (known as direction-dependent effects), creating imaging artefacts ("grating lobes") that obscure fainter sources and mimic the cosmological signal. To overcome this, the authors reprocess a 24-hour observation of the North Celestial Pole from the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA) over 75–175 MHz using a new direction-dependent calibration pipeline (`21CMAcali`) combined with full electromagnetic simulations of the antenna primary beam. By partitioning the sky into 10 directional facets and modelling the ultra-bright radio galaxy 3C 61.1 as two components, they significantly suppress sidelobe artefacts and construct an improved foreground catalogue of 1246 radio sources, providing a cleaner baseline for subtracting foregrounds in future 21-cm power-spectrum analyses.

papers.title: Weighing dark matter particles with gravitational waves
papers.authors: Rodrigo Vicente, Francisco Duque, Theophanes K. Karydas, Gianfranco Bertone
papers.abstract: It is commonly assumed that the mass of dark matter particles cannot be determined from their gravitational effects when dark matter behaves as collisionless matter. Here we show that extreme-mass-ratio inspirals observable by millihertz gravitational-wave observatories such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) could measure the mass of ultralight dark matter particles in sufficiently dense dark matter spikes. The separation of scales between the two black holes allows ultralight dark matter to form a collisionless density spike around the massive primary while retaining wave effects in its interaction with the stellar-mass companion. We incorporate wave-dependent accretion and dynamical friction into relativistic inspiral waveforms and jointly infer the dark matter particle mass, spike normalisation and binary parameters from simulated LISA signals. For massive black holes at the low-mass end of the LISA population ($M\sim 10^5 M_\odot$), our forecasts show that particle masses spanning $10^{-14}-10^{-11}\,\mathrm{eV}$ could be measured to within an order of magnitude.

conclusions: The inner density and environmental torque profiles of adiabatically grown dark matter spikes have a nearly universal radial shape within $r \leq 30 R_M$, allowing the host halo dependence (for initial cusp slopes $0.25 \leq \gamma \leq 1.5$) to be captured by a single normalization parameter $\bar{\rho}$ to within $5\%$ accuracy.

For a fiducial low-mass LISA EMRI ($M = 2\times 10^5 M_\odot$, $m = 18 M_\odot$, $\mathrm{SNR}=50$ over 3 years) in a reference spike, two-sided Bayesian constraints recover the dark matter particle mass within an order of magnitude for $m_\phi \sim 10^{-13}\text{--}10^{-12}\,\mathrm{eV}$, where the spike induces $30\text{--}2000$ cycles of orbital dephasing.

Outside this "Goldilocks" mass window, wave effects either saturate onto a long-wavelength plateau ($m_\phi \lesssim 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{eV}$) or converge to the classical point-particle limit ($m_\phi \gtrsim 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{eV}$); in the heavy limit, the particle mass only gets a lower bound, though the spike density itself is still measured to better than $1\%$ precision.

Achieving an order-of-magnitude mass measurement for heavier primaries ($M = 4\times 10^5 M_\odot$) requires either a steep initial baryonic/dark matter cusp ($\gamma = 1.5$), high signal-to-noise ($\rho_{100\,\mathrm{pc}} \propto \mathrm{SNR}^{-(4-\gamma)}$), or extending the observation from 4 to 8 years to sample wider orbital separations ($21\text{--}24 R_M$) where environmental drag is stronger relative to gravitational radiation.
ai.summary: Normally, purely gravitational observations can only map out the macroscopic density of collisionless dark matter, leaving the mass of individual dark matter particles completely degenerate. This paper shows how extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs)—where a stellar-mass black hole slowly spirals into a massive $10^5\text{--}10^7 M_\odot$ black hole over hundreds of thousands of orbits—can break this degeneracy for ultralight bosonic dark matter using the future space-based gravitational-wave detector LISA. Because of the huge scale separation between the two black holes, a scalar particle with a Compton wavelength between their respective horizon scales behaves like a classical collisionless particle around the central supermassive black hole (forming a dense "spike"), but acts like a quantum wave when scattering off and accreting onto the smaller companion. By building this wave-dependent gravitational drag (dynamical friction) into relativistic EMRI waveforms and running Bayesian MCMC forecasts, the authors demonstrate that the radial profile of the drag depends on the particle mass, allowing LISA to simultaneously weigh the dark matter particle and measure the spike's density.

papers.title: Measuring the magnetization profiles of galaxy groups and clusters
papers.authors: Kritti Sharma, Vikram Ravi, Elisabeth Krause
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields are vital in determining the physical conditions of baryons in massive halos. They are, however, notoriously difficult to observe. This impacts problems from our understanding of galaxy formation, to the observed deficit in the amplitude of thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) power spectrum that affects cosmological inferences. Although Faraday rotation measures (RMs) offer a direct probe of magnetic fields, it weights magnetic fields by the free-electron density. Several probes of free electrons, including fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures (DMs) and kinematic SZ (kSZ) effect, are now maturing into precision tools. We combine RM$^2$ stacks from SPICE-RACS around DESI galaxy groups and ROSAT clusters with optical depth profiles constrained jointly by the FRB DM-redshift relation and the kSZ effect, and obtain 95% upper limits on the rms line-of-sight magnetic field of $<3.9$-$11.6~\mu$G ($<2.3$-$6.4~\mu$G) in groups (clusters) for a 10~kpc coherence length. Combining these with thermal pressure profiles inferred from tSZ-shear cross-correlations, we obtain 95% lower limits on the plasma $\beta$ of $>0.31$ ($>11$) in groups (clusters). Although current constraints are only limits, we forecast a first detection with larger datasets from the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA). We present the first forecast of the DSA RM grid density ($\sim365$ RMs deg$^{-2}$), which when combined with 10$^4$ FRBs would measure the field in groups to $3$-$13\%$ precision, compared to current constraints of $38$-$75\%$. Although the interpretation of current measurements remains challenging owing to depolarization along turbulent halo sightlines and the unknown coherence length, larger samples and DSA/Square Kilometer Array observations may resolve these uncertainties by measuring polarization-fraction profiles and the RM structure function using extended radio sources, respectively.

conclusions: Stacked $\mathrm{RM}^2$ profiles around DESI BGS groups and RASS clusters are detected at total significances of $1.9\sigma$ and $3.6\sigma$, respectively; assuming a $10\text{ kpc}$ field coherence length ($l_c$), this yields $95\%$ upper limits on the root-mean-square line-of-sight magnetic field of $B_{\parallel,\mathrm{rms}} < 3.9\text{--}11.6\,\mu\text{G}$ in groups and $< 2.3\text{--}6.4\,\mu\text{G}$ in clusters (scaling as $l_c^{-1/2}$).

Combining these magnetic field bounds with thermal gas pressure profiles yields $95\%$ lower limits on the plasma beta ($\beta \equiv P_{\mathrm{th}}/P_B$) of $\beta > 0.31$ in groups and $\beta > 11$ in clusters for $l_c = 10\text{ kpc}$ (scaling linearly with $l_c$), meaning magnetic pressure in clusters is at most $\sim 10\%$ of the thermal gas pressure.

Compared to the IllustrisTNG magnetohydrodynamical simulation, the observed cluster $\mathrm{RM}^2$ profile lies significantly below simulated predictions despite matching the electron column density; the authors attribute this primarily to Faraday depolarization selection effects, where background radio sources behind dense, turbulent cluster cores lose polarization and drop out of the catalog.

Forecasts for the upcoming Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), expected to provide $\sim 365\text{ RMs deg}^{-2}$ ($>10^6$ sources) alongside $10^4$ localized FRBs, show that the fractional precision on effective group magnetic fields will improve from $38\text{--}75\%$ today to $3\text{--}13\%$, while its $3''$ beam will help measure the field coherence length directly.
ai.summary: Magnetic fields in galaxy groups and clusters play a key role in regulating baryonic feedback and providing non-thermal pressure support, which could help explain why the observed thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) power spectrum—a measure of hot gas thermal pressure—is systematically lower than theoretical predictions. However, measuring these fields using Faraday rotation measures (RMs, which track how a magnetic field rotates the polarization angle of background radio light) suffers from the "baryon-magnetism degeneracy": the RM signal is an integral of the magnetic field multiplied by the free-electron density along the line of sight. To break this degeneracy without suffering from sign cancellation or noise bias, the authors stack squared residual rotation measures ($\mathrm{RM}^2$) from $\sim 2.5 \times 10^5$ ASKAP SPICE-RACS polarized radio sources around 15.4 million DESI Bright Galaxy Survey groups ($\bar{M}_{200c} \sim 10^{13.3} M_\odot$) and 7,775 ROSAT X-ray clusters ($\bar{M}_{200c} \sim 10^{14.4} M_\odot$). By combining these $\mathrm{RM}^2$ stacks with independent electron column density profiles—constrained jointly via fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures and kinematic SZ (kSZ) data—and thermal pressure profiles from tSZ–cosmic shear cross-correlations, they place direct observational bounds on halo magnetic field strengths and the ratio of thermal to magnetic pressure (plasma $\beta \equiv P_{\mathrm{th}}/P_B$).

papers.title: Sym-EFT: Accelerating Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure with Symbolic Regression
papers.authors: Despoina Farakou, Constantinos Skordis
papers.abstract: We present an emulator suite for the one- and two-loop cold dark matter power spectrum from the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structures (EFTofLSS). Specifically, we emulate separately the various contributions to the one- and two-loop parts of the power spectrum, leaving out the possible counterterms which can be added as multiplicative prefactors. By leaving the time-dependence of the counterterms unspecified at the emulation stage, our technique has the advantage of being extremely versatile in fitting any type of counterterm parametrisation to data, or to simulations, without having to change the emulator. We construct our emulators using the method of symbolic regression which results in functions that can be used directly in computer code, while achieving errors of better than $0.5\%$ within the $k$-range of validity of EFT and maintaining ultra-fast computational evaluation of less than $\sim5\times10^{-4}s$ on a single core.

papers.title: Heavy Black-Holes Also Matter in Standard Siren Cosmology
papers.authors: Grégoire Pierra, Alexander Papadopoulos
papers.abstract: With the release of the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog GWTC-4.0 by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration, 218 candidate detections of gravitational waves (GWs) from compact binary coalescences (CBCs) have been reported. This milestone represents a major advancement for GW cosmology, as many methods, particularly those employing the spectral siren approach, critically depend on the number of available sources. We investigate the impact of a novel parametric model describing the full population mass spectrum of CBCs on the estimation of the Hubble constant. This model is designed to test the impact of heavy black holes in GW cosmology. We perform a joint inference of cosmological and population parameters using 142 CBCs from GWTC-4.0 with a false alarm rate smaller than 0.25 per year, using both spectral and dark siren approaches. With spectral sirens, we estimate the Hubble constant to be $H_0 = 78.8^{+19.0}_{-15.3}\,{\rm km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1}}$ (68% CL), while the dark siren method yields $H_0 = 82.5^{+16.8}_{-14.3}\,{\rm km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1}}$ (68% CL). These results improve the uncertainty by approximately 30.4% and 36.2%, respectively. We show that this improvement is linked to the presence of a new mass scale in the binary black hole mass spectrum at $63.3^{+4.8}_{-4.8}\,M_{\odot}$, which provides additional constraints on the Hubble constant. Besides providing the tightest standard-siren constraints on $H_0$, this highlights the importance of a heavy-mass feature in the black hole spectrum.

papers.title: Extracting intrinsic alignments in the Dark Energy Survey's year 1 data, using the self-calibration method and LSST-DESC tools
papers.authors: Eske M. Pedersen, Leonel Medina-Varela, Emily Phillips Longley, Mustapha Ishak, Joe Zuntz, Chihway Chang, C. Danielle Leonard (for the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (LSST DESC))
papers.abstract: We present the implementation of a Self-Calibration of Intrinsic Alignments of galaxies as an extension to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC)'s weak lensing 3x2pt pipeline (TXPipe). As a demonstration, we have run this pipeline on the Dark Energy Survey (DES) year one data set. We find indications of a non-zero intrinsic alignment signal in the higher redshift bins, while in the lower bins our results look more uncertain. We believe this is caused by known issues with the individual galaxies photo-z estimation. This effect is particularly harmful for the self-calibration method, since it has high requirements for reliable estimation of the photo-$z$s, and the need for individual galaxy point estimates and tomographic binning to match. We show how different methods of recreating the redshift probability distribution can affect the detection of intrinsic alignment.

papers.title: Increasing the Precision of Surrogate Models for Weak Lensing Mass Maps with Flow Matching
papers.authors: Guangjian Li, Tomasz Kacprzak
papers.abstract: Weak gravitational lensing maps compactly encode the evolution of cosmic large-scale structure and are a key tool for cosmological analyses. Performing inference directly at the map level allows flexible choices of statistics and can increase constraining power. Conventional methods rely solely on N-body simulations and are computationally expensive. Generative machine-learning emulators can accelerate map-level theory prediction. However, existing GAN-based map-level surrogates still have limited statistical fidelity. They can produce over-smoothed maps, may fail to capture the full distribution of generated map sets and can be difficult to train. Continuous normalizing flows trained with flow matching have recently emerged as a powerful class of generative models. We present a residual label-conditional flow matching generative network that conditions explicitly on the matter density $\Omega_m$ and clustering amplitude $\sigma_8$ for a fixed source redshift distribution $n(z)$. The model learns a continuous probability flow in a residual space from label-specific noise distributions to convergence maps. We evaluate it using pixel and peak statistics, the power spectrum, bispectrum, power-spectrum correlation matrices, and other validation metrics. Compared with the previous GAN benchmark, the proposed method improves the typical fidelity of generated maps from below 10% and below 20% to below 1% and below 5% for basic and higher-order statistics, respectively. The agreement at the level of map distributions is also very good: maps generated from random noise match well the distribution of maps generated with N-body simulations from random initial conditions. This work brings us closer to a practical mass-map emulator that captures the cosmological signal while supporting multiple forms of data analysis.

papers.title: Pushing the Primordial Frontier: Exact Linear Solutions in Multifield Inflation
papers.authors: Javier Huenupi, Claudio Muñoz, Gonzalo A. Palma, Spyros Sypsas
papers.abstract: We present exact analytic solutions for the linear dynamics of a two-field inflationary system in which the primordial curvature perturbation $\zeta$ is coupled to an isocurvature perturbation $\sigma$ of entropy mass $\mu$. The solutions are valid for arbitrary values of $\mu$ and the dimensionless interaction strength $\lambda$. They therefore provide analytic control over the strong mixing regime in which $\zeta$ interacts with light isocurvature fields, commonly associated with rapid-turn inflation.
